sens: A grand sumptuous meal to which many guests are invited
A moment of celebration and joy around an abundant table
H3900.detail: 1. A feast is a large, rich, and generous meal where many people gather to celebrate an important occasion. In Daniel 5:1, King Belshazzar organizes a great feast for a thousand of his nobles, a royal and solemn event. 2. The feast evokes the idea of joy, abundance, and conviviality: it is a time when people rejoice together, where food and drink flow freely, and where a festive atmosphere prevails.
H3900.origine: This Aramaic word (the language spoken by the Jews in exile in Babylon) is related to the Hebrew 'lechem' (לֶחֶם), which primarily means "bread" or "food." In Aramaic, the same word comes to designate the feast itself — no longer the isolated food, but the complete meal, the entire occasion of eating together. This is a natural shift: from the concrete (the bread) to the context (the set table, the feast).
H3900.emploi: This word appears only once in the Scriptures, in Daniel 5:1, where it describes the royal banquet of Belshazzar. It is an Aramaic term, specific to the passages of Daniel and Ezra written in this language (rather than Hebrew). Its use here emphasizes the grand and royal nature of the event, before the mysterious hand appears and writes God's judgment on the wall.
H3900.portee: This feast reminds us that the feasts of the world, even the most magnificent, remain temporal and can be interrupted by divine judgment. For the believer, this invites us not to place our trust in earthly pleasures, but to seek first the Kingdom of God.

sens: armed combat, conflict between peoples or armies
trial, threatening danger
H3901.detail:
1. The word denotes armed combat: a direct confrontation between warriors or peoples. In the Song of Deborah, when Israel has "neither shield nor spear" in the face of "war at the gates" (Judges 5:8), it refers to a concrete, imminent, and terrifying military threat. This is the most direct and material sense of the word.
2. By extension, the word can evoke a trial, a danger that assails: any situation of hostility or peril. Here, "the war was at the gates" describes not only a military event but also the threat looming over the people and endangering their existence.
H3901.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of walking, going to battle, confronting. The word belongs to the concrete vocabulary of ancient life, where armed conflicts were common and determined the fate of peoples. The exact meaning remains debated by scholars, but it clearly refers to situations of combat and military tension.
H3901.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the Song of Deborah (Judges 5:8). This historical context recounts the early days of Israel under the judges, a troubled time when external threats were constant. The poem highlights the imminence of military danger and emphasizes the people's vulnerability in the face of this threatening enemy.
H3901.portee: This verse reminds us that in the face of the perils that assail the people of God, help does not come from armament or human strength, but from God alone. In the context of the Song of Deborah, it is after imploring the Lord that victory comes. The word "war" also speaks to the Christian conscience of the spiritual battle that accompanies the life of faith.

sens: Giant of Gath, brother of Goliath
Enemy of Israel defeated by a Hebrew warrior
H3902.detail:
1. Lahmi is a giant from the city of Gath, brother of the famous Goliath and son of Rapha. He appears in the account of Israel's military exploits under the united monarchy, where he is among the giants that God's people faced.
2. Lahmi was killed in battle by Elhanan, son of Jair, one of Israel's warriors. This episode shows how God granted victory to His people even against formidable and oversized enemies.
H3902.origine: The name Lahmi literally means "my bread" in Hebrew, probably a nickname or a familiar expression whose precise origin escapes us. He belongs to the family of giants from Gath, descendants of Rapha, like his brother Goliath. This name reminds us that even the most impressive adversaries in the Bible are named and known by God.
H3902.emploi: Lahmi appears only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 20:5, where he is mentioned as the brother of Goliath and as the man whom the Hebrew warrior Elhanan defeated in battle. This brief account is part of the series of victories of Israel over the giants, showing how God protected His people against the most formidable enemy powers.
H3902.portee: The story of Lahmi reminds us that no earthly force, however imposing, escapes God's control. Like Goliath, his brother, the defeat of this giant assures the reader that God grants victory to His people, even when the enemy seems invincible. It is an invitation to trust in God rather than fear seemingly insurmountable obstacles.

sens: city in the lowland of Judah
H3903.detail: Lachmas is a small city located in the coastal plain of southern Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible. It appears in the list of cities that Joshua distributed to the tribe of Judah during the allocation of the promised territory (Joshua 15:40).
H3903.origine: The name Lachmas means "provisions" or "food" in Hebrew, likely evoking a place of resources or supply. This name reflects the agricultural importance of this fertile region of the Judean plain.
H3903.emploi: Lachmas appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:40, as one of the many cities listed during the allocation of territory among the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan. It is classified among the cities of the lowland (Shephelah), a fertile region between the hills of Judah and the Mediterranean coast. Its appearance in an administrative list shows that it was a recognized locality, though of little importance to the point that the Bible gives us no further information about it.

sens: Woman living with a powerful man without being his legal wife
Relationship of lower status than that of a wife, but recognized and lasting
Historical practice of kings and prominent figures in the ancient Near East
H3904.detail:
1. A concubine is a woman who lives marital with a man, particularly a king or a prominent figure, but without having the legal status of a wife. She occupies an intermediate position: recognized in the household, but subject to a social hierarchy. The three occurrences in the book of Daniel (5:2, 5:3, 5:23) mention her alongside the king's wives, thus distinguishing two categories of women in the royal palace.
2. This status reflects a reality of the royal courts of the ancient Near East. A king had one or more official wives, mothers of his heirs, and concubines who also formed an organized group in his household. It was an accepted practice, even if inferior to marriage.
3. In the context of Daniel 5, the concubines participate in royal feasts and are part of court life, which shows their established, albeit secondary, place in the palace hierarchy.
H3904.origine: The Hebrew word לְחֵנָה (lechénah) comes from a root meaning "embrace" or "lodging" — the idea of a woman who shares a man's bed. This name thus designates a stable intimate relationship but lacking the legal status of marriage. The practice was common in Mesopotamian and Egyptian royal courts.
H3904.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, all in the same account (Daniel 5:2, 5:3, 5:23): the description of the banquet of King Belshazzar on the eve of the fall of Babylon. Each time, it enumerates the three categories of women present — wives, concubines, and perhaps others — to show the scale and splendor (or impiety) of the royal feast. The term primarily serves to paint a picture of Babylonian court life.
H3904.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not hide the customs of pagan cultures, nor those of Israel. It speaks of them without explicitly condemning the person, but situates this practice in a context of distancing from God. In the passage from Daniel, the accumulation of royal pleasures — gold, wine, women — symbolizes the pride and forgetfulness of God that precede judgment.

sens: To exert physical pressure on something or someone
To push someone or something away by force
To overwhelm someone under the weight of mistreatment or unjust domination
H3905.detail:
1. The verb primarily denotes a physical action: to squeeze, press, compress. This is the basic meaning of the Hebrew word, like squeezing something in one's hand or against an obstacle.
2. It can also mean to push someone away by force. In Judges 1:34, the Amorites "pressed back" the sons of Dan, meaning they forced them to leave a territory by exerting physical and military pressure.
3. However, the most common meaning in the Bible is spiritual and moral: to oppress, that is, to subject someone to cruel and unjust domination. In Exodus 3:9, God sees "the oppression that the Egyptians cause them to suffer" — a constant, inhumane pressure that crushes the people. The Pharaoh weighs down on Israel like a crushing burden. This weight can also be that of affliction: in Psalms 56:2, the psalmist says that his adversaries "continually oppress" him, tormenting him without respite.
H3905.origine: The Hebrew root לחץ (la-khats) evokes an action of compression or constriction: to press, to squeeze. It is related to the physical idea of applying pressure. The word conveys the image of a force that crushes or weighs heavily — first literally (pressing something), then figuratively (overwhelming a person). In the Greek Septuagint, it is often translated by a verb that also means "to oppress" or "to afflict."
H3905.emploi: The verb appears about eighteen times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical books (Judges, Samuel, Kings) and in the Psalms. It most often describes the domination that one people or king exerts over another: the Egyptians oppress Israel (Exodus 3:9), Jabin oppresses the children of Israel with his iron chariots (Judges 4:3), enemies oppress Israel under divine judgment (Psalms 106:42). Sometimes it refers to direct military or physical pressure (Judges 1:34: the Amorites press back the sons of Dan). The Torah also uses it to exhort justice: do not oppress the foreigner (Exodus 23:9), for Israel itself suffered as a foreigner in Egypt. Each time, the word carries the idea of an overwhelming and intolerable force.
H3905.portee: This word reminds us that oppression is a serious evil in the eyes of God. The Bible emphasizes the suffering of the oppressed and the responsibility of those who abuse their power. God hears the cry of those who are crushed (Exodus 3:9) and intervenes to deliver them. This speaks to the heart of the Christian: compassion for the marginalized, the weak, and the persecuted is not just a feeling, but a moral requirement rooted in the love of God who defends the voiceless.

sens: The action of crushing someone, submitting them by force
The state of one who suffers from pressure, an unbearable burden
The pain or distress that results from it
The bread and water given to a prisoner to keep them weak
H3906.detail:
1. Oppression is primarily the action of crushing a people under the weight of domination: the Egyptians oppressed Israel in Egypt (Exodus 3:9), and later the king of Syria oppressed Israel with all his might (2 Kings 13:4). It is a weight that crushes from above downwards.
2. The word also denotes the state of one who undergoes this pressure: it is the condition of suffering, the oppression that Israel endures, which they cry out to God to be delivered from (Deuteronomy 26:7). The oppressed breathe poorly, as if crushed.
3. Oppression can also be inner suffering, the grief that overwhelms the soul (Job 36:15: God warns through suffering the one He saves). It is a moral distress.
4. In royal prisons, captives are given bread and water of affliction to weaken and subdue them (1 Kings 22:27, 2 Chronicles 18:26): an intentional deprivation that prolongs the oppression.
H3906.origine: The Hebrew word לַחַץ comes from a root that evokes the idea of squeezing, pressing, crushing under a weight. The starting image is physical: to compress, to apply pressure. It is a verb and a noun from the same family that both express the action of reducing someone to helplessness by a superior force.
H3906.emploi: The word appears ten times in the Old Testament, mainly to describe the political domination of one people over another or of a king over his prisoners. In the narratives of the people of Israel, oppression refers to the servitude in Egypt (Exodus 3:9) and foreign invasions (2 Kings 13:4). The king imposes oppression in prison by reducing the captive to the minimum (1 Kings 22:27). In the Psalms (42:10, 43:2, 44:25), oppression becomes the expression of all moral distress, which the psalmist cries out to God. In Job 36:15, the suffering of oppression becomes God's instrument to warn and correct. The meaning always focuses around crushing and unbearable weight.
H3906.portee: This word helps the believer recognize that God sees and hears those who suffer under injustice and domination. When the Bible speaks of oppression, it affirms that this suffering is not hidden from God: He sees it (Exodus 3:9, 2 Kings 13:4) and acts to deliver. It is a word of hope for those who live under the weight of injustice.

sens: To speak very softly, in a low and restrained voice
To practice magic, enchantment, or divination through mysterious words
To murmur to oneself, exchanging secret words
H3907.detail:
1. The primary meaning is simply to speak in a very low voice, by whispering. In 2 Samuel 12:19, David sees his servants speaking "softly" among themselves and understands without being explicitly told that the child is dead: they whisper, which is enough for him to grasp the gravity of the situation.
2. By extension, the word also refers to those who practice magic, enchantment, or divination — often murmuring enigmatic words or incantations that are supposed to have occult power. Psalm 58:6 speaks of the "most skillful magician," who, through his mysterious words, claims to bind or unbind powers.
3. The underlying idea is that of a confidential murmur, of secret exchanges whispered among oneself, as if transmitting secrets or hidden formulas.
H3907.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the sound of whispering, of muffled speech. The same family of words produces names for those who practice these secret words: "charmers," "magicians," "diviners." The basic image is that of a low and mysterious voice, often associated with the attempt to master or influence invisible powers through ritual words.
H3907.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Old Testament. In 2 Samuel 12:19, it simply denotes the act of speaking softly. In the Psalms (41:8 and 58:6), it is used to describe magicians and enchanters who call upon occult powers, revealing how the Bible views these practices: enigmatic murmurs, often linked to forbidden sorcery or divination. The context always shows a form of secrecy, mystery, or even spiritual danger.
H3907.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible acknowledges the existence of magical practices and those who engage in them, while warning against them: enchanters possess no real power against the living God. Whispering secret formulas to control the spiritual realm is a dangerous illusion. The believer finds strength and protection only in God, not in the whispers of magicians.

sens: whisper, murmur
the act of charming or conjuring (especially snakes)
one who practices this art
amulet or magical object worn on oneself
prayer or whispered supplication
H3908.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the whisper or murmur, this act of speaking softly and in a restrained voice — for example, the low voice of a prayer (Isaiah 26:16).
2. By extension, it refers to the action of charming, particularly the art of conjuring snakes through supposed magical formulas or gestures: in Ecclesiastes 10:11, the snake that bites "because of enchantment" evokes the idea that one believed they could neutralize a snake through a kind of whispered charm.
3. One who practices this enchantment is called an "enchanter": in Isaiah 3:3, it refers to a particular artisan, counted among the important men of the city.
4. The word also refers to the magical objects themselves, the amulets that women wore as talismans of protection (Isaiah 3:20).
5. In a higher spiritual sense, it is the prayer itself, understood as a fervent supplication whispered to God in distress (Isaiah 26:16).
H3908.origine: The root evokes whispering, the discreet murmur — the basic image is that of a low voice that buzzes or murmurs. In Hebrew, this whisper naturally shifted towards the idea of magical charm, as it was imagined that magicians conjured snakes with mysterious words whispered. The same word could thus refer to both the whisper of a prayer and a magical formula, depending on the context.
H3908.emploi: This word appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the prophets. In Ecclesiastes and Jeremiah, it concerns the enchantment of snakes: these were supposed to obey the charms of the enchanters, which was a pagan belief that Scripture does not validate but mentions as a practice of the idolatrous world. In Isaiah 3, it refers both to the enchanter as an urban profession and to the amulets worn by vain women. In Isaiah 26:16, the same word takes on a positive spiritual value: a whispered "prayer" in distress. Thus, the Bible takes a word from magical vocabulary and applies it to true prayer.
H3908.portee: This word reminds us that the temptation of men is always to seek a magical or hidden power to control life and nature — snakes, diseases, dangers — rather than to trust in God. At the same time, the use of the word for "prayer" shows that true power lies in the confident supplication addressed to the Lord, not in powerless charms. The Christian can see a lesson here: to abandon all recourse to occult practices and instead seek the face of God.

sens: Secret art or mysterious practice by which one claims to produce extraordinary effects
The act of doing something discreetly, without noise or haste
Discretion, reserve in speech or action
H3909.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to enchantment, that is, a hidden, mysterious know-how by which the Egyptian magicians claimed to perform wonders. In Exodus 7:22, Pharaoh's magicians "did the same by their enchantments" by imitating the plagues that Moses caused: enchantment here is an occult practice meant to rival the power of God, even though it can ultimately only mimic.
2. The word can also describe an action carried out discreetly, without noise. Ruth 3:7 shows this when Ruth "came quietly" to Boaz who was asleep: she acted with caution and reserve, lightly, so as not to disturb him. Similarly, in 1 Samuel 24:5, David "cut off the corner of Saul's robe quietly" while he was sleeping: the gesture is secret, deliberate, almost furtive.
3. Finally, the word can mean confidence, that is, a confidential word, a speech held in secret or with reserve. In 1 Samuel 18:22, Saul orders his servants to "speak confidentially to David," meaning to speak to him privately, discreetly, to entice him.
H3909.origine: The Latin word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of what is hidden, secret, not apparent. It is related to other Hebrew terms meaning "secret" or "whisper" (like latash, "to whisper"). The basic image is that of the hidden, the discreet, that which is done without witness or fanfare. This root is rooted in the concrete experience of secrecy, whispering, action carried out in darkness or silence.
H3909.emploi: The word lat appears six times in the Hebrew Bible. Three occurrences are found in the accounts of the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 7:22; 8:3; 8:14) where it refers to the enchantments of the Egyptian magicians who attempt to counterfeit Moses' miracles: here the word carries a nuance of imposture, of supposedly magical occult power. Two occurrences show it in the sense of discretion, gentleness (Ruth 3:7 and 1 Samuel 24:5): Ruth approaches Boaz gently, David discreetly cuts Saul's garment. A final occurrence (1 Samuel 18:22) uses it for a word held in confidence, a secret conversation. The word thus navigates between two poles: on one side, the occult secret, almost malevolent (magic); on the other, the benevolent secret, prudent discretion.
H3909.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible discerns true power from false. The Egyptian enchantments, despite their impressive appearance, can only mimic the miracles of the living God: they reveal human pride that claims to equal the Creator. Conversely, discretion and reserve — when they serve to protect, as Ruth shows — can be virtuous and necessary. The word teaches us to discern the deceptive secret from the protective secret.

sens: An aromatic natural resin extracted from a shrub in Arabia
A precious substance used as perfume or incense
A valuable commercial commodity
A gift or valuable present
H3910.detail:
1. Myrrh is a fragrant resin produced by a small shrub from the Middle East: it oozes from the bark and hardens into golden and shiny beads. It is a highly valued natural substance, almost as precious as gold to the ancients (Genesis 37:25).
2. Its intense fragrance makes it a sought-after ingredient for ointments, incense, and cosmetics: the caravaners passing through the Promised Land transport it to sell in Egypt, at the rich markets of the Nile Valley.
3. Myrrh is traded as a highly valuable commodity: merchants load their camels with myrrh, balm, and spices, as these natural treasures yield great profit in distant trade.
4. Used as a gift or present, myrrh signifies respect or gratitude: Israel advises his sons to take some to the Egyptian vizier as proof of the honor they wish to show him (Genesis 43:11).
H3910.origine: The Hebrew word לֹט likely comes from an ancient Semitic root meaning a substance that flows or oozes — the image of resin dripping from the tree. It is a very ancient product: the Egyptians already used it for mummification, and it appears in the earliest accounts of Genesis as a coveted item. The name itself evokes the idea of abundance and exchange: where there is myrrh, there is trade, wealth, and the foreigner.
H3910.emploi: The word appears twice in Genesis, in commercial contexts. First in Genesis 37:25, where the Ishmaelite merchants carry it along with other spices to Egypt: it is a picture of mercantile activity and Eastern wealth. Then in Genesis 43:11, where Israel advises his sons to take it as a present to the Egyptian governor: myrrh then becomes a sign of respect and a means of establishing relationships. In both cases, it embodies value, exoticism, and luxury from the ancient Levant.
H3910.portee: Myrrh reminds the reader that God makes the Promised Land rich in precious goods and resources sought by distant nations. It also illustrates how material goods, however beautiful, are means for human relationships and survival: Israel accepts to submit by offering these treasures to save his family. It is a subtle lesson on the hierarchy of values in the believer's heart.

sens: Un unidentified reptilian animal
Creature declared unclean by Mosaic law
H3911.detail:
1. The Hebrew word לְטָאָה refers to a creeping creature, probably a small to medium-sized reptile. The exact animal cannot be determined with certainty: it could be a variety of lizard, a chameleon, or an extinct species. The Segond translates it as "turtle" (Leviticus 11:30), indicating that the translator was uncertain about the precise identification.
2. This creature appears in the list of unclean animals in the Israelite dietary law (Leviticus 11:30). It is listed alongside the hedgehog, the frog, and the snail, all of which are forbidden for consumption by the people of Israel. The unclean status marks a ritual separation: these animals must not be touched or eaten.
H3911.origine: The Hebrew word לְטָאָה comes from a root that expresses the idea of "creeping" or "leaping," as it refers to a small animal that moves by crawling on the ground. The family of this word includes other names of reptilian or creeping animals in the Bible. The exact word remains opaque in its distant origins, but its function is clear: to designate a small reptile that Israel was to avoid ritually.
H3911.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Leviticus 11:30, in the context of the law of the clean and unclean given to Moses. It is included in a list of creeping animals considered unclean: the hedgehog, the frog, this creature (translated as "turtle"), the snail, and the chameleon. This list fits within the system of ritual purification that distinguishes the Israelites and orders them to respect holy boundaries between the clean and the unclean, the holy and the common.
H3911.portee: This word reminds us that the Mosaic law sanctified every detail of daily life, including diet, to teach Israel an obedience that engages the whole body. For the Christian, this law finds its fulfillment in Christ: it no longer isolates the believer with dietary prohibitions but calls them to be holy in heart and life (cf. 1 Corinthians 10:25-26). This word invites us to reflect on the freedom that Christ grants us in relation to external observances.

sens: People descended from Letush, son of Dedan
H3912.detail: The Letuschim are a people or clan mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 25:3. They descend from Letush, son of Dedan, who is himself the son of Jokshan and the great-grandson of Abraham through his second wife Keturah. They are listed alongside the Aschurim and the Leummim as brothers, meaning as related peoples stemming from the same ancestor Dedan.
H3912.origine: The name Letuschim comes from Letush and etymologically means "the hammered ones" or "those who have been forged," a suggestive image that could evoke a shaped or robust people. This name fits within the genealogy of ancient Arab peoples descended from Abraham and Keturah.
H3912.emploi: The Letuschim are mentioned only once in Scripture, in Genesis 25:3, in the context of the genealogy of the sons of Dedan. They appear in the list of eastern peoples contemporary to Israel, as historical and genealogical information, without being the subject of any particular narrative or action.

sens: make sharp by rubbing or hammering
forge, hammer metal to make a tool or weapon
cause a sharp wound, a penetrating pain
H3913.detail:
1. To sharpen means to make a blade or instrument sharp by rubbing or striking it. In 1 Samuel 13:20, the Israelites went down to the Philistines to sharpen their agricultural tools — plows, mattocks, axes — which they had to maintain regularly.
2. To forge refers to the work of metal with a hammer: in Genesis 4:22, Tubal-Cain was the one who forged all the instruments of bronze and iron, meaning he shaped them by hammering to make useful tools.
3. Figuratively, "to sharpen" one's sword (Psalms 7:13) or one's tongue (Psalms 52:4) means to prepare an attack, a hurtful word: one sharpens their weapon or malice as one sharpens a blade to pierce more deeply. In Job 16:9, "piercing" with the gaze expresses this same idea of a sharp and painful attack.
H3913.origine: The Hebrew verb latash comes from a root that evokes the sound and action of a hammer or rubbing — the primary image is that of working metal or stone by percussion or friction. This word has no common Greek or Latin equivalent; it designates a specifically Hebrew action, that of the artisan who shapes. The root carries the idea of creating through repeated and violent work.
H3913.emploi: This verb appears five times in the Old Testament, mostly to speak of manual work: forging metal tools (Genesis 4:22), maintaining and sharpening agricultural instruments (1 Samuel 13:20). Alongside this concrete and artisanal use, the Bible employs it figuratively to describe the preparation of a weapon or a word intended to wound: sharpening one's sword for battle (Psalms 7:13), honing a deceitful tongue (Psalms 52:4). In Job 16:9, the gaze that "pierces" refers to the same image of the sharpened instrument that penetrates and wounds.
H3913.portee: This word reminds us that our words and intentions can be sharpened like blades — they pierce and wound all the more as they are carefully prepared. The image of the blacksmith working metal with patience also emphasizes that evil, like good, is often built through repetition and habit. For the believer, this invites vigilance over what they prepare and say, recognizing the destructive power of a word honed by malice.

sens: Ornament that hangs or wraps around an architectural structure or object
Decorative motif in the form of a garland or chain
H3914.detail:
1. A festoon is a decorative element that hangs or wraps around, particularly around the bases, panels, or posts of a construction. In Solomon's Temple, they can be found beneath and above the lions and oxen that adorn the bronze bases (1 Kings 7:30), as a supplement of beauty to these massive structures.
2. It also refers to a garland or a decorated frieze that extends around a surface: the plates of the supports of the bronze basin were thus adorned with cherubim, lions, palms, and garlands all around (1 Kings 7:36). It is a relief or pendant motif that enriches architectural elements.
H3914.origine: The Hebrew word לֹיָה (loyah) has an uncertain meaning and etymology. It specifically designates suspended or wrapped ornaments and appears only in descriptions of the sacred furniture of the Temple. The form of the word and its context of use suggest an element of decoration in relief or garland.
H3914.emploi: The word loyah appears only three times in the Bible, all in the first book of Kings, chapter 7, which describes in detail the bronze furniture of Solomon's Temple. It is found in the descriptions of the movable bases and the basin, where it designates the festoons or garlands that complement the carvings of lions, oxen, and cherubim. These ornaments hung between the posts or wrapped around the structures, adding richness and elegance to these pieces of sacred craftsmanship.
H3914.portee: This word reminds us that Solomon's Temple was not only a place of worship but also a demonstration of splendor and beauty: every detail, down to the smallest ornaments like the festoons, was designed to manifest the glory of the God of Israel. This invites the reader to see that excellence and beauty in the execution of service to God are never trivial details, but reflect the honor given to God.

sens: The period of darkness between sunset and sunrise
The moment or duration measured in successive nights
Midnight or an hour during the night
Figuratively: moral darkness, a time of distress or trial
H3915.detail:
1. Night is the time of day when darkness and gloom prevail, in contrast to the light of day. Genesis 1:5 shows this primary opposition: God separates the light (day) from the darkness (night), with both alternating regularly. This is the natural cycle of creation.

2. To measure a duration, nights are counted: "forty days and forty nights" (Exodus 24:18) signifies a complete period, day and night. When the Bible speaks of several successive nights, it is the entirety of the elapsed time that matters.

3. "Midnight" designates the heart of the night, the middle of the period of darkness (Judges 16:3). This precise hour often marks a decisive or dramatic moment in the narratives.

4. Night also symbolizes a situation of trial, anguish, or moral uncertainty. Job 36:20 warns against the desire for night as a deceptive refuge. Isaiah 15:1 uses night as a symbol of imminent destruction and ruin.
H3915.origine: The Hebrew word laïlah comes from a root that evokes darkness and what covers. In Hebrew, night dominates the natural cycle since the Hebrews counted days "from evening to evening": night came first, which is why many biblical narratives situate decisive events at night (dreams, divine appearances, escapes). Night is never a mere physical phenomenon: it is the place where God acts and speaks in a hidden manner.
H3915.emploi: The word "night" appears more than 220 times in the Hebrew Bible, notably in Genesis, Exodus, and Judges. It primarily denotes the period of natural darkness (Genesis 1:5, Exodus 13:21-22), but also the nights spent in watchfulness, prayer, or suffering (Exodus 24:18: Moses forty days and nights on the mountain). Often the Bible reports that God appears or acts at night: prophetic dreams (Genesis 20:3, 26:24, 46:2), divine signs (Exodus 12:12, 14:20). Night can also express a hidden action (Joshua 2:2, Judges 6:27) or a moment of hasty escape (2 Kings 8:21: Joram rises at night). It sometimes becomes a symbol of crisis or threat (Isaiah 15:1).
H3915.portee: For the believer, the biblical night is never the absence of God but often the privileged place of His action and revelation. It teaches that God remains active in the dark moments of our lives, when everything seems hidden. It also invites us to vigilance and trust: even when all is darkness, God watches over us (Deuteronomy 1:33, where the pillar of fire guides at night).

sens: the moment of darkness between sunset and sunrise
a vision or experience received during sleep or in darkness
H3916.detail:
1. Night is the time of darkness when the sun has disappeared. In Daniel 5:30, it is "that very night" that King Belshazzar is killed — the word simply denotes the moment of darkness. Daniel 2:19 recounts that "the secret was revealed to Daniel in a vision during the night": it is the natural setting where God speaks to His prophets in their dreams.
2. The word also takes on a more symbolic hue: it designates the state of vision, the mystical experience received in darkness and silence. When Daniel says, "I was watching in my night visions" (Daniel 7:2, 7:7, 7:13), the word "night" qualifies the visions themselves, the revelations that come at night. It is the context in which God shows His servant hidden realities and distant futures.
H3916.origine: The Hebrew word לֵילָא (layil) comes from a root that literally means "to be dark" or "to enter into darkness." In biblical Hebrew, it simply designates night as part of the natural day. In Aramaic — the language of the book of Daniel — it retains this primary meaning, but night also becomes the privileged setting for prophetic visions, a moment when the barriers between the visible and the invisible thin.
H3916.emploi: This word appears five times, all in the book of Daniel, in Aramaic. Four times it qualifies Daniel's visions ("night visions" in 7:2, 7, 13), once it simply situates the event in time (the death of Belshazzar in 5:30). Night is not a trivial detail: it is the sacred hour when the invisible God reveals Himself to the prophet. Daniel receives in these visions the succession of the kingdoms of the world and the announcement of the Son of Man who will judge history.
H3916.portee: For the believing reader, this emphasis on the night of visions reminds us that God often speaks in darkness, silence, and intimacy. It is an encouragement to seek His voice beyond the noise of the day, and to recognize that what seems dark or incomprehensible may be the place of His most precious revelations.

sens: Supernatural being or nocturnal animal that haunts desolate places
Demon or female specter associated with darkness and desolation
H3917.detail:
1. This word designates a creature that lives at night and frequents abandoned and barren places. In Isaiah 34:14, in a vision of judgment on Edom, the text evokes a specter or nocturnal animal that will find its dwelling and rest among the ruins — an image of complete desolation, where even the strangest and most fearsome creatures will settle.
2. The term can also refer to a demon or a spirit of darkness, a figure from ancient mythology that represents all that is hostile to life, light, and the created order. It is a hostile presence that symbolizes chaos and divine abandonment.
H3917.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "night" (layil), and designates what belongs to the night or originates from it. It refers to a creature or entity associated with darkness, likely influenced by Mesopotamian or Canaanite traditions regarding nocturnal demons. The word can refer either to a real but mysterious animal that inhabits only at night, or to a supernatural being.
H3917.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 34:14, in a prophetic passage describing the destruction and desolation of Edom. Here, it figures among other creatures of wild and abandoned places — desert animals, wild dogs, goats — suggesting that it is either a real and little-known nocturnal animal or a demonic creature. The context clearly indicates that it is a dweller of ruins, a sign that the place is completely given over to abandonment and divine destruction.
H3917.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible acknowledges the existence of dark powers hostile to the created order, and that God's judgment can reduce lands to a state of desolation such that even the strangest and most fearsome creatures will find refuge there. It is a biblical image of punishment: not only death and ruin, but also the absence of divine blessing and the reign of chaos.

sens: Large carnivorous feline from hot and arid regions
Symbol of strength and courage
Image of power and danger
Figure of evil or destructive threat
H3918.detail:
1. The lion is a large feline that lives in the desert and semi-arid regions of the Near East. It is a powerful predator that hunts for food: Job 4:11 reminds us that "the lion perishes for lack of prey," showing that even this king of beasts depends on hunting for survival.
2. The lion represents impressive strength and absolute mastery over other creatures. Proverbs 30:30 refers to it as "the mightiest among beasts, which does not turn back before any," embodying courage and fearlessness in the face of any adversary.
3. Due to its fearsome and unpredictable nature, the lion becomes a biblical image of danger and the threat that looms over the weak. Isaiah 30:6 associates it with other menacing creatures of the desert, among the perils faced by those traveling in hostile lands.
4. In biblical texts, the lion often symbolizes evil that seeks to devour, destructive power, or tyrannical domination — an image that evokes sin or the enemy threatening God's people.
H3918.origine: The Hebrew word yish comes from a root that expresses the idea of strength and power. The lion was well known to the ancient Israelites, who often used it in their texts as a living symbol of what is violent, insurmountable, and majestic. The word frequently appears in biblical poetry to enhance the impression of grandeur or terror.
H3918.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible according to the provided usages. It appears in poetic contexts (Proverbs, Isaiah, Job) where it serves to amplify an idea: sometimes that of the very fragility of powerful creatures in the face of lack of prey (Job), sometimes that of the absence of fear in one who reigns supreme (Proverbs), and sometimes that of the lurking danger in hostile lands (Isaiah). The lion remains a figure of absolute power and potential threat.
H3918.portee: For the Christian reader, the lion reminds us that even the most impressive forces of the visible world are subject to limits and to the will of God. This image also helps to grasp the biblical allusions to sin or the spiritual adversary as a formidable power but defeated by faith. It invites recognition of God's strength in contrast to the threats of this world.

sens: Ancient city in northern Israel, located in Upper Galilee
Meaning "lion" in Hebrew
H3919A.detail: Laïs is a city in northern Israel, in Upper Galilee, that the Danites conquer and rename Dan during the time of the judges (Judges 18:29). It bears the name "lion" in Hebrew, which evokes either the strength and ferocity of the region or the importance of the city. At the time of its conquest, Laïs was inhabited by a peaceful and prosperous people, without organized military defense, living apart from the rest of the country (Judges 18:7, 18:27). The Danites, in search of territory, seize it after massacring its inhabitants and burning the city, then rename it Dan in honor of their ancestor (Judges 18:29).
H3919A.origine: The name Laïs comes from the Hebrew word for "lion" (yish), a feared and prestigious animal. This name reflects either the ancient importance of the city or the characteristics of the territory. The city will change its name to become Dan, named after the patriarch Dan, son of Jacob (see Dan H1835G). This city later becomes a major geographical landmark in Israel: the region "from Dan to Beersheba" will refer to the entire territory of the kingdom.
H3919A.emploi: Laïs appears only in the account of Judges 18, which tells of the migration of the tribe of Dan to the north. It first appears as an object of exploration (Judges 18:7, 18:14), then as a target of conquest (Judges 18:27), before being renamed Dan (Judges 18:29). The text emphasizes that it was an isolated city, prosperous but vulnerable, without defensive alliances. After its conquest and burning, Laïs ceases to exist under that name; the tribe of Dan would make it the northern sanctuary of Israel, where a rival cult to that of Jerusalem would be established.
H3919A.portee: This passage illustrates how cities and places receive their names according to their history: Laïs, the city of the lion, disappears under that name when it is conquered and renamed. This reminds us that the names of places and peoples are never neutral — they tell a story, that of those who lived there and those who transformed them. For the Christian reader, it is also an example of how the tribe of Dan would establish its own religious practices, far from the centralized worship prescribed by the Law.

sens: Father of Palti, a man during the united monarchy
Man to whom King Saul betrothed his daughter Michal
H3919B.detail: Laïsch is the father of Palti (or Palthiel), a man from the royal house of King Saul. Although Michal, Saul's daughter, was married to David, Saul gave her in marriage to Palti, son of Laïsch (1 Samuel 25:44). This situation shows how Saul attempted to separate his daughter from David and diminish the influence of the future king. After Saul's death, Saul's son, Ish-Bosheth, ordered Michal's husband, Palthiel son of Laïsch, to return the young woman to David (2 Samuel 3:15). Laïsch himself is never directly mentioned in the narrative: he is known only as the father of Palti, who is involved in the dramas of Saul's court.
H3919B.origine: The name Laïsch means "lion" in Hebrew, an image of strength and power. It is a spelling variant of the name Lush (לוּשׁ). The name was borne in the lineage of a man close to Saul's royal family.
H3919B.emploi: Laïsch is mentioned only twice in the Bible, both times in relation to his son Palti. In 1 Samuel 25:44, he is identified as the father of the man to whom Saul gave Michal. In 2 Samuel 3:15, the same Palthiel, son of Laïsch, is ordered to reclaim Michal to return her to David. These two references place him in the political context of the rivalry between Saul and David, although he is never a principal actor in the reported events.

sens: City in northern Judea
Stopover for the Assyrian army
H3919C.detail: Laïs is a small city located north of Jerusalem, heading north (Galilee). Its name means "lion" in Hebrew, suggesting its strategic location or the strength of its inhabitants (Isaiah 10:30). In the only biblical passage that mentions it, the prophet Isaiah lists the cities that the Assyrian army passes through or threatens during its advance, calling out Laïs as a place that cannot escape divine judgment.
H3919C.origine: The name Laïs derives from the Hebrew laïsh, which means "lion." It is a descriptive name, common in the regions of the Levant to designate strong or formidable places. The same Hebrew word also appears as a proper name for other biblical localities.
H3919C.emploi: Laïs appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 10:30. It is included in the list of cities that the prophet enumerates to show the progression of the Assyrian army (around 701 B.C.) descending toward Jerusalem. The context is that of divine judgment on Judah: Isaiah addresses these cities as if they were hearing the warning. Laïs, though small, is significant because it lies on the path of the invader, showing that no place, even humble, escapes judgment.
H3919C.portee: This passage reminds believers that God's plans concern the entirety of the territory: no city, no person is hidden from His sight. Laïs, though obscure, is named; this invites the reader to meditate on divine sovereignty over every corner of land and every life.

sens: To seize a city or fortress by force
To capture a person, to take them prisoner
To be captured, to fall into a trap or ambush
To designate someone by drawing lots
To grasp, to hold something or someone
To figuratively seize someone (by temptation, sin)
H3920.detail:
1. To seize a city or fortress by force: this is the most common meaning. When an army "takes" a city, it becomes master of it through conquest. Example: "In the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria took Samaria, and carried Israel away captive to Assyria" (2 Kings 17:6).
2. To capture a person, to take them prisoner: the word refers to the act of seizing someone, often in war or during an ambush. Example: "Let them be taken in the net which they have hid" (Psalms 35:8).
3. To be captured, to fall into a trap or ambush: the passive form of the verb describes one who undergoes the action, who falls into the power of an enemy or danger. In Job it is said: "The cords of iniquity surround him" (Job 36:8).
4. To designate someone by drawing lots: this is a rarer but important usage. God uses the casting of lots to identify the guilty party. Example: "Joshua took the people, tribe by tribe" (Joshua 7:14).
5. To grasp, to hold something or someone: the verb can simply mean "to take" or "to hold" in a more neutral sense.
6. To figuratively seize someone, by temptation or sin: example: "The wicked woman... will take you like a game" (Proverbs 5:22).
H3920.origine: The Hebrew verb לָכַד comes from a root that literally means "to seize" or "to catch." The word evokes the image of a hand closing around something. It belongs to the family of verbs of violent action or capture. In ancient Hebrew, this verb is used for all types of seizing: that of the hunter capturing his prey, that of the soldier seizing a city, or that of God holding someone in the net of His justice.
H3920.emploi: This verb appears 112 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the historical books (Joshua, Judges, 1 and 2 Samuel, 1 and 2 Kings, 1 and 2 Chronicles) where it describes the military conquests of Israel during the time of the Conquest and the monarchy. There are also uses in the wisdom literature (Proverbs, Job) in a figurative sense. When it comes to cities, the verb is almost always military: one "takes" Jerusalem, Samaria, Jericho. When it comes to people, it can mean capturing an enemy in battle ("taking" kings) or being caught in a trap (Psalms 35:8). In a figurative sense, in Proverbs, it expresses how sin or the strange woman "takes" a man in its nets. The casting of lots in Joshua 7 is a particular case where God "takes" or "designates" the guilty party.
H3920.portee: This word reminds the reader of the reality of the conquests and wars that God led to give Israel the promised land. It also shows us, in the figurative passages, how sin functions like a trap: it "takes" the one who approaches it. For the Christian, this invites vigilance and understanding that God has the power to "take" or "seize" — both to judge and to save. It is a verb of power and mastery, revealing either military strength, the cunning of evil, or the authority of God.

sens: A trap set to capture someone or something
Danger or misfortune prepared against someone
H3921.detail:
1. The trap is primarily a physical device set to capture prey or an enemy. It is an ambush, a snare. In Proverbs 3:26, it speaks of preserving one's foot from any trap: the image evokes someone walking without falling into the traps set along their path.
2. By extension, the trap becomes any form of hidden danger or misfortune that someone prepares against us — a temptation, a trial, a moral or spiritual trap. It is an evil that one does not see coming.
H3921.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to capture" or "to take." It expresses the idea of seizing, catching someone off guard. The same family gives words for loot or capture in hunting and war.
H3921.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Proverbs 3:26. It is a classic term of biblical wisdom for speaking of hidden dangers that threaten the righteous on their path. In this context, it is the Lord who protects and preserves from these traps: it is an act of divine guarding, of benevolent vigilance.
H3921.portee: This verse reminds that the believer is never left to themselves in the face of the dangers of the world. The Lord is a reassurance, an active protection: He keeps us from visible and invisible traps. It is an invitation to trust in God rather than in our own strength, knowing that the dangers we do not see are in His hands.

sens: City of Judah
Son of Er and grandson of Shelah
H3922.detail:
1. Leka is a city in the territory of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible in connection with the families of artisans who worked there, notably those who made fine linen, a precious fabric.
2. Leka is also the name of a man from the tribe of Judah, son of Er and grandson of Shelah, living during the time of the divided monarchy. He is mentioned in the genealogy of Judah as the father of Mareshah.
H3922.origine: The Hebrew word לֵכָה (lekah) literally means "journey" or "way," an image that can evoke a place of passage or transit. This name, borne both by a city and by a man from the tribe of Judah, reminds us how ancient Hebrews often gave their cities and descendants names that carried spiritual or geographical significance.
H3922.emploi: Leka appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:21, in the detailed genealogy of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy. The context shows that Leka was a place associated with families of artisans specialized in the making of fine linen, a luxurious fabric used in priestly garments and royal clothing. This mention reveals the economic and artisanal importance of certain places in Judah.

sens: Fortified city in southern Judah, conquered by Joshua
H3923.detail: Lachish is a fortified city located south of Jerusalem, on the borders of the territory of Simeon. It originally belonged to the Amorites before being conquered by Joshua during the conquest of Canaan and integrated into the territory of the tribe of Judah (Joshua 10:31-32). The city played an important strategic role: it served as a base for the Assyrian kings during their siege of Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:17), and it was a refuge for King Amaziah who perished there (2 Chronicles 25:27). Its military importance is confirmed by its frequent mention in accounts of campaigns and wars.
H3923.origine: The name Lachish literally means "invincible," which likely reflects the idea of an impregnable fortress. This city was well known in ancient Egypt and Assyria, as shown by historical sources and modern archaeological discoveries.
H3923.emploi: Lachish appears 22 times in the Bible, primarily in the historical books. It is first mentioned in the account of the conquest of Canaan by Joshua (Joshua 10:3, 10:31-34), where it is taken after a siege. During the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, it remains a strategic fortified city: it is mentioned in the list of cities of Judah (Joshua 15:39), and later in the wars against Assyria where it becomes a stronghold for Assyrian troops (2 Kings 18:17; Isaiah 36:2). It is also the place where King Amaziah takes refuge before being assassinated there (2 Chronicles 25:27).
H3923.portee: Lachish illustrates how God gives His people fortified cities and strongholds. Its history also shows that even the best-defended cities cannot withstand when God acts for His people: Joshua takes it easily by divine power. Later, its role in the Assyrian invasions reminds us that without faithfulness to God, no fortress truly protects.

sens: Loop or textile ring used to join two elements
Assembly element of the curtains of the Tabernacle
H3924.detail:
1. The lace is a small loop of fabric made on the edge of a cloth. In the Tabernacle, God commands Moses to make blue laces on the edge of the curtains (Exodus 26:4): these are rings or loops attached to the edge of the fabric, which serve to tie together two pieces of cloth.
2. The specific use of the lace in the Tabernacle is to assemble the curtains together. Fifty laces are prepared on the edge of one curtain and fifty on the edge of another, so that "these laces will correspond to each other" (Exodus 26:5). Then, bronze clasps (bronze hooks) are passed through these laces to securely join the two curtains and form the covering of the Tabernacle (Exodus 26:11).
H3924.origine: The Hebrew word לוּלַי (loulai) specifically refers to a loop or a handle. Its root evokes the idea of wrapping, bending, forming a curve. The word appears almost exclusively in the description of the construction of the Tabernacle, where it is one of the precise details that shows how God gave the plans for His sanctuary to the people of Israel.
H3924.emploi: The word lace appears only 7 times in the Bible, all in Exodus 26 and 36, at the heart of the instructions for building the Tabernacle. Exodus 26 states God's order; Exodus 36 recounts how Bezalel and the craftsmen executed this order. The lace has only one function: it is the concrete means of joining together the ten curtains of fine linen that form the main veil of the Tabernacle. Its importance is underscored by the precise number (fifty on each side) and its color (blue), which corresponds to the color code of the sanctuary.
H3924.portee: The lace reveals how God cares about detail, down to the small fabric ring. Nothing is left to chance in the Tabernacle: every loop, every color, every number carries meaning and contributes to the harmony of the whole. For the believer, this teaches that God pays attention to the meticulous and that faithful obedience in the details, even the humblest, honors the Lord.

sens: To transmit knowledge or understanding to someone
To receive knowledge, to acquire understanding
To train someone through practice or exercise
To accustom someone to something
H3925G.detail:
1. To teach is to actively transmit knowledge, a law, or a skill. God teaches Israel His laws and statutes so that the people may understand and practice them (Deuteronomy 4:1). It is the action of a master who intentionally communicates what he knows.
2. To learn is to receive this transmission and accumulate it within oneself. Israel was to learn warfare, meaning to acquire combat experience (Judges 3:2). This is the passive aspect of the same act: the one who receives the teaching.
3. To exercise or train means to form someone in a skill through repeated practice. God trains hands for battle, making them capable and skillful through use (Psalms 18:35). The word evokes learning through experience, not just through words.
4. To instruct through discipline or warning: chastening and teaching go together, as correction itself is a form of teaching. God instructs through His law so that man may understand what is right (Psalms 94:12).
H3925G.origine: The root לָמַד (la.mad) originally means "to sharpen" or "to make fit," hence "to learn" and "to teach." The basic image is that of shaping: just as one sharpens a tool, one hones the mind and skills through learning. The word appears in various forms in Hebrew (to learn, to teach, to be taught), and it has been used to translate into Greek the same ideas of transmission and acquisition of knowledge.
H3925G.emploi: The verb לָמַד appears about 60 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Pentateuch and the Psalms. In Deuteronomy, it describes Israel's obligation to learn and practice the laws of the Lord (Deuteronomy 4:1, 4:5, 4:10). The Psalms make extensive use of it: the psalmist asks God to teach him (Psalms 119:135), to help him understand His statutes and judgments. In 1 Chronicles 25:7, it refers to musicians trained in the singing of the Lord. The word can also describe physical or military training (Psalms 18:35; Judges 3:2). Among the prophets like Jeremiah and Isaiah, it often highlights Israel's refusal to learn or listen to divine teaching (Jeremiah 32:33; Isaiah 48:17).
H3925G.portee: This word reminds the believer that knowledge of God is not innate: it must be learned, it is a gift that is received with humility. Biblical teaching is not a mere transmission of information; it is a formation of the entire life, a practical application and training of the heart. Knowing who God is and what He expects requires listening, receiving, and allowing the Word to transform us.

sens: To acquire knowledge or skill through study or instruction
To retain a moral or spiritual lesson through experience or adversity
To observe and imitate what others do
To teach or transmit knowledge (active sense: to make learn)
H3925H.detail:
1. The most common meaning is this: to receive knowledge, to gradually assimilate it. In Deuteronomy 4:10, the people summoned by God must "learn to fear me" — this means acquiring awareness of the living God by listening to His words. Learning also involves memorizing and understanding (Deuteronomy 17:19: the king reads the law "so that he may learn to fear").
2. Adversity itself can "teach" us — it can instruct the heart in ways that mere words cannot. In Psalm 119:71, the psalmist says: "It is good for me that I was afflicted, that I may learn your statutes"; suffering becomes a teacher of divine wisdom.
3. To learn can also mean "to imitate" or "to adopt the customs of." Psalm 106:35 speaks of Israel mingling with the peoples and "learning their works" — that is, taking pleasure in their practices contrary to God.
4. The verb can take the active voice ("to make learn") or passive voice ("to be taught"). Isaiah 1:17: "Learn to do good" — a call to progressively acquire justice by practicing it.
H3925H.origine: The Hebrew word lamad (לָמַד) comes from a root that expresses the idea of "to direct towards," "to train," "to lead." It is the image of a master guiding the steps of a student. The verb also exists in Aramaic with the same meaning. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), this verb corresponds to Greek words like "manthanô," which also means "to learn." The root suggests a progressive movement, a formation that requires time and perseverance.
H3925H.emploi: The verb "to learn" appears 22 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of Moses (Deuteronomy), the Psalms, and the Prophets. It primarily describes religious instruction: learning to fear God (Deuteronomy 4:10; 5:1), learning His laws (Psalms 119:71). But it also extends to the imitation of bad practices: learning the customs of neighboring peoples (Deuteronomy 18:9; Jeremiah 10:2), which serves as a warning. The prophets use it to call the people to "learn justice" (Isaiah 1:17), and sometimes to note the failure of those who refuse to learn (Isaiah 26:10: "the wicked does not learn justice"). The verb always emphasizes a process, a gradual acquisition.
H3925H.portee: For a believer, this word reminds us that faith is never complete: it requires a discipline of constant learning of the Word and ways of God. Learning to fear the Lord means building one's life on the foundation of His revelation. But the word also warns: one can learn evil just as well as good (imitating idols, adopting the sins of the world). Finally, it indicates that adversity itself can become a school if we welcome it with humility — suffering can teach us what we could never learn otherwise.

sens: with a view to, intended for
in the presence of, before
inside of, in
in contact with, on
H3926.detail:
1. With a view to, intended for: the word indicates the purpose or destination of an action. Job 27:14 states that the children of the wicked are "for the sword," meaning they are destined to perish by the sword.
2. In the presence of, before: it marks the position of an observer or witness. Job 29:21 recounts that people kept silent "before" Job's counsel, meaning in front of him, attentive to his words.
3. Inside of, in: it situates something within a place or state. Job 39:2 asks if wild animals are lying in wait "in" their den.
4. In contact with, on: it expresses a relationship of contact or immediate proximity. Job 39:37 states that Job puts his hand "on" his mouth as a sign of silence and respect before the greatness of God.
H3926.origine: This word is a short poetic form of the inseparable Hebrew preposition לְ (le), which is one of the most common prepositions in Hebrew. The preposition fundamentally expresses a relationship or link: toward, to, for. Here, the short vowel and the contraction עוֹ make it a particular variant in the poetic style of the book of Job. This preposition attaches directly to the following word and modifies its nuances according to the context.
H3926.emploi: This word appears four times in the book of Job, the quintessential poetic text of the Hebrew Bible. In Job 27:14, it introduces the unfortunate destination of the wicked's children; in Job 29:21, it spatially situates the context of a respectful audience; in Job 39:2, it localizes wild animals; in Job 39:37, it marks the gesture of the hand covering the mouth. All these uses show that the preposition, in its poetic form, functions exactly like its more common variant: it connects a verb or noun to its complement by specifying a relationship of purpose, place, or contact.
H3926.portee: Noticing this poetic form invites recognition that biblical poets carefully chose their forms for rhythm and depth. This preposition, omnipresent in Hebrew, weaves the logical and spatial links of the text; understanding its nuances helps grasp how the Bible expresses relationships between beings, places, and actions. It is a reminder that every word counts, even the smallest ones.

sens: A king to whom his mother addresses teachings
H3927.detail: 1. Lemuel is an unknown king from the Old Testament to whom his mother imparts maxims of wisdom. These teachings form a section of the book of Proverbs (Proverbs 31:1-31), where the king's mother instructs him on the conduct a ruler should maintain, notably warning him not to drink wine or seek strong drinks (Proverbs 31:4).
H3927.origine: The name Lemuel means "for God" or "dedicated to God" in Hebrew. It is a proper name that appears only in the book of Proverbs. Some commentators have suggested that Lemuel might be a nickname or another name for Solomon, but there is no certainty about this.
H3927.emploi: Lemuel is mentioned twice in the Bible, both times in chapter 31 of the book of Proverbs. He first appears in verse 1 as the king whose mother conveys her words of wisdom to him, and then in verse 4 in one of those teachings, where his mother urges him to abstain from wine. He is primarily a literary character in the context of Hebrew wisdom literature.

sens: One who receives teaching and learns from a master
A tongue or ear trained to perform its function well
Accustomed to something, habituated to a practice, a habit
H3928.detail:
1. A disciple is one who has been taught and receives the discipline of a master. In Isaiah 54:13, the prophet announces that all sons will be "disciples of the Lord," meaning they are trained and instructed by God Himself to know His ways.
2. The word can designate what has been shaped by habit and regular training — a trained tongue is one that practice has made skillful and effective. In Isaiah 50:4, the servant speaks of a "trained tongue" that God has given him to comfort the weary, and of an "ear" formed to listen like disciples do.
3. One who is "accustomed" or "habituated" to something has been shaped by repetition until it becomes second nature. In Jeremiah 2:24, the wild donkey is "accustomed" to the wilderness; in Jeremiah 13:23, the inhabitants of Jerusalem are "accustomed" to doing evil as a second nature.
H3928.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally means "to learn" or "to be taught." It describes the process by which someone receives training, instruction, or becomes accustomed to a practice through repetition. The central notion is that of transformation through teaching or habit: one becomes a disciple by being trained, one becomes accustomed through practice.
H3928.emploi: This word appears five times in the Old Testament, primarily in the writings of the prophet Isaiah and in Jeremiah. In Isaiah, it first designates the disciples of the prophet (Isaiah 8:16), then those who listen as disciples (Isaiah 50:4), and finally all the sons that God will form for Himself (Isaiah 54:13). The meaning then extends to the state of being accustomed or habituated: in Jeremiah, the word describes the wild donkey accustomed to the wilderness (Jeremiah 2:24) and the people accustomed to doing evil (Jeremiah 13:23). In all cases, it carries the idea of an inner transformation produced by teaching or repetition.
H3928.portee: This word invites the believer to see themselves as a disciple of God, that is, as someone whom God continually forms and transforms. It also shows the power of habit: one becomes what one regularly practices. The Christian is called to be a disciple of the Lord, formed and instructed by Him, rather than being "accustomed" to evil as Jerusalem was.

sens: Man of the lineage of Cain before the Flood
Son of Methushael and father of Jabal, Jubal, and Tubal-cain
Man characterized by violence and vengeance
H3929G.detail:
1. Lamech is a character from the Old Testament, living before the Flood. He belongs to the lineage of Cain, the first murderer, and embodies the escalation of violence in pre-flood humanity (Genesis 4:18).
2. He is the son of Methushael and the father of three significant sons: Jabal, the inventor of livestock; Jubal, the inventor of music; and Tubal-cain, the inventor of metallurgy. He also has a daughter, Naamah.
3. Lamech is primarily known as the man who breaks the divine limit regarding vengeance. He kills for his wound and his bruise, then proclaims that his vengeance will surpass that of Cain: where Cain is avenged seven times, Lamech will be avenged seventy-seven times (Genesis 4:23-24). This enormous number symbolizes an overflow of unrestrained violence.
H3929G.origine: The name Lamech means "powerful" in Hebrew. It reflects a power that, in this character, is expressed through physical strength and vengeance. Lamech represents a turning point: while his sons invent and build civilization, he illustrates the violent heart of carnal humanity. His name and story form a contrast with the wisdom of his descendants in the arts and techniques.
H3929G.emploi: Lamech appears four times in Genesis, always in chapter 4, which recounts the story of the lineage of Cain. He is first presented as a member of this genealogy (Genesis 4:18), then as a man married to two women, Ada and Zillah (Genesis 4:19). The text then shows him confessing his crime: he has killed a man and a young man, and he boasts about it to his wives, urging them to listen to him (Genesis 4:23). Finally, he states his disproportionate law of vengeance (Genesis 4:24). Lamech symbolizes the man who refuses the limits that God imposes on vengeance, embodying the sin that thrives before the judgment of the Flood.
H3929G.portee: The account of Lamech warns the reader that unrestrained violence and personal vengeance are a revolt against divine order. God alone is judge; the man who takes justice into his own hands places himself outside of God's law. Lamech's trajectory — from crime to boasting — shows how sin hardens the heart and leads man to glorify himself in evil. It is a lesson on the consequences of rejecting grace.

sens: Man who lived before the Flood, father of Noah
H3929H.detail: Lamech is the son of Methuselah and the father of Noah. He appears in the genealogy of humanity before the Flood, as one of the ten patriarchs who lived for very long years. According to Genesis 5:28-29, he fathered a son at one hundred eighty-two years and lived to be seven hundred seventy-seven years old. He represents a link in the chain of humanity's transmission from Adam to Noah, the one chosen to survive the Flood.
H3929H.origine: The name Lamech means "powerful" in Hebrew. It designates a major figure in the antediluvian genealogy: the ninth patriarch after Adam and the direct father of Noah. His name appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Seth, reported in Genesis 5 and reiterated in 1 Chronicles 1.
H3929H.emploi: Lamech is mentioned six times in the Bible, only in Genesis 5:25-31 and 1 Chronicles 1:3. All references place him in the genealogical line connecting Adam to Noah. Genesis 5:25-26 introduces him as the son of Methuselah, Genesis 5:28 reports that he fathered Noah, and Genesis 5:30-31 provides the numbers of his exceptional life. 1 Chronicles 1:3 simply restates his name in the summary of the antediluvian generations. His role is limited to that of a genealogical link: he represents the transmission of human life before the Flood.

sens: The front part of the neck through which food and air pass
Figuratively, the capacity to eat or drink without restraint
H3930.detail:
1. The throat is the front part of the neck, the narrow passage through which food and air we breathe descend. It is the organ that swallows and breathes. In Proverbs 23:2, the expression "put a knife to your throat" is a striking image: it invites one with an insatiable appetite to exercise self-control, as if they must stop the act of eating by placing a weapon against this passage. This illustrates how violent the desire to overeat can be and how firm one must be against oneself.
2. Figuratively, the throat also represents the immoderate desire for enjoyment — here, the greed for food. One who devours without restraint surrenders their throat to covetousness; the text warns that this servitude is serious and requires constant vigilance.
H3930.origine: The Hebrew word לֹעַ is a variant or rare form of vocabulary related to the human body. It specifically designates the passage through the neck where life — food and breath — transit. It is a very concrete term, without abstraction: it names the organ as one sees and feels it when swallowing or breathing.
H3930.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Proverbs 23:2. It is part of a series of wise counsel directed at young people: "Put a knife to your throat, if you have too much greed." The image of the knife against the throat expresses the urgency of mastering one's gluttonous impulses. The context is clearly one of temperance and self-control in the face of temptations of lust or gluttony that threaten the soul of the wise.
H3930.portee: This passage shows us that Proverbs takes seriously the inner struggle against carnal appetites. The throat — a symbol of all that enters us through desire — reminds us that our body is a spiritual battleground. The Christian, like the wise man of Israel, must learn to say no to greed, to reign over their own passions, for the absence of self-control opens the door to all evils.

sens: To make jokes, mockeries to ridicule someone
To treat with derision and contempt, to refuse to take seriously
H3931.detail:
1. The word describes the action of making jokes or mockeries — the way of mocking someone through words or laughter, seeking to turn them into a laughingstock. In 2 Chronicles 36:16, the Israelites "mocked the messengers of God," which shows that one mocks a person, not a thing.
2. On a deeper level, it is to refuse to treat someone with respect, considering them unworthy of being listened to. When one mocks, they implicitly reject what the other says; in the same verse, this mockery goes hand in hand with contempt for the words of God and derision towards the prophets — it is an act of spiritual rebellion that despises divine authority.
H3931.origine: The Hebrew word primarily denotes the action of joking or scoffing. The form used here (Hiphil) intensifies the idea: to make mockeries, to begin mocking. This root expresses disdain through words — turning someone into a laughingstock rather than listening to them.
H3931.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 36:16, in a crucial historical and theological context. The passage describes the successive generations of Israel who rejected the prophets: first by despising them, then by mocking them, which shows an escalation of sin. This mockery is presented as a serious form of rebellion against God, provoking His anger until it becomes "without remedy." It is a deliberate act of rejection, not a mere triviality.
H3931.portee: This rare occurrence reminds the reader of the spiritual danger of disdain towards the word of God. To mock is not a light sin: it is to refuse to listen, it is pride that does not want to submit. The passage invites respect for God's message and His messengers, and warns against the gradual hardening of the heart that begins with contempt and leads to destruction.

sens: To express contempt for someone by laughing at them or turning them into a laughingstock
To manifest one's mockery through insolent gestures or words
To persist in ridiculing someone despite their protests
H3932.detail:
1. To mock someone is to publicly insult them by laughing at them, by showing contempt. The virgin daughter of Zion "mocks" the enemy who threatens her (2 Kings 19:21): she is not afraid, she scorns him. Those who see Jesus on the cross "mock" Him, opening their mouths and shaking their heads (Psalms 22:8), a gesture of derision and defiance.
2. To mock can also refer to the physical attitude or words through which one manifests their contempt: Sanballat and his companions "mocked" those who were rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 2:19), addressing them with insolence. It is an attack intended to humiliate and discourage.
3. Sometimes, mockery persists or intensifies: Job fears that his accusers will "mock" him with impunity (Job 11:3). It is an active, repeated contempt that harasses its victim.
H3932.origine: The Hebrew verb לָעַג comes from a root that evokes the idea of turning into ridicule, publicly humiliating through words or gestures. It carries the image of someone who diverts the respect owed to others to make them an object of derision. The word belongs to the lexical field of contempt and insolence, distinct from simple benevolent mockery.
H3932.emploi: The verb appears eighteen times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms, Job, and historical books. It describes the attitude of enemies or wicked people towards the righteous and the servants of God. In the Psalms (22:8, 59:9, 80:7), the psalmist asks God to cease delivering him to those who mock him. Job complains of being the laughingstock of his accusers (11:3, 22:19). Nehemiah reports how his adversaries mocked him during the rebuilding of the walls (2:19, 4:1). The word expresses not a mere joke, but a hostile and persistent contempt, often linked to opposition to God's project or His servants.
H3932.portee: This word shows us that the contempt of men has always accompanied the servants of God. Jesus Himself was mocked on the cross. Recognizing that this is the fate of the faithful helps the believer not to be surprised or discouraged by the hostility of the world. But it is also a call to moral vigilance: the Bible warns us against our own tendencies to mock others, especially those who are weak or marginalized (Proverbs 17:5).

sens: Word or attitude that mocks someone
State of one who is the object of mockery
Ridicule, derision
H3933.detail:
1. Mockery is primarily an act: speaking or acting in a way that ridicules someone. It is to scoff, to openly mock. Job drinks "mockery like water," meaning he is constantly inundated by his companions who ridicule him.
2. It is also the state of one who suffers this mockery: to become a mockery is to be exposed to the ridicule and contempt of others. The mountains of Israel have become "a laughingstock to other nations" — they symbolize a humiliated people turned into derision.
3. The word finally denotes the contempt and disgrace that accompany mockery. The psalmists speak of the mockery of the proud and the haughty: it is an active contempt, a will to belittle.
H3933.origine: The Hebrew word לַעַג (la'ag) comes from a root expressing the idea of mocking or scoffing at someone. The same root appears in other contexts of mockery or derision in the Old Testament. It always depicts an attitude of hurtful mockery.
H3933.emploi: This word appears 7 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Psalms and in the prophets. It describes situations where Israel or individuals suffer contempt: the neighbors of Israel mock the people of God (Psalms 44:14; 79:4), the proud ridicule the humble (Psalms 123:4). Ezekiel uses it to describe the humiliation of the nations. The context always shows that mockery is a form of disgrace — it hurts and humiliates. In Job 34:7, mockery targets a righteous man, showing the injustice of those who mock.
H3933.portee: This word reminds us that mockery and ridicule are a form of moral violence. The psalmists teach us to take seriously the contempt that faith can provoke: following God sometimes exposes one to ridicule. But this word also encourages us: God sees the mockery we endure, and it will not go unanswered. It is a call to patience and trust in Him who judges.

sens: One who mocks, who scoffs with disdain
One who speaks in a strange or incomprehensible manner
H3934.detail:
1. The mocker is a person who scoffs and harms through their words or attitude. In Psalms 35:16, the psalmist describes "mocking parasites" who gnash their teeth against him — the image is that of someone openly displaying their contempt and hostility through ridicule and derision.
2. The word can also refer to one who speaks in an unintelligible or strange manner, as another form of mockery or confusion. In Isaiah 28:11, the Lord threatens to speak to the people through people "with stammering lips" and in a barbarous language — not that God Himself stutters, but that He will send foreigners whose incomprehensible language will be a judgment and mockery for the rebellious people.
H3934.origine: The word הָעֵג comes from a root expressing the idea of diverting, deviating, or speaking in a distorted manner. The basic image is that of a twisted word or an attitude that mocks by distorting reality. It is a rare word in Hebrew, used to designate both the mocker and one who speaks in a strange or incomprehensible manner.
H3934.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Psalms 35:16, it qualifies hostile individuals who mock the psalmist with disdain. In Isaiah 28:11, the same word describes the lips of those who will speak a foreign and incomprehensible language — not as true mockery, but as a form of divine judgment where intelligibility is lost. In both cases, it evokes a word that hurts or confuses.
