H3934.portee: This word reminds us that mockery is a weapon of evil that deeply wounds, and that God Himself can use misunderstanding and confusion as judgment against those who reject His word. The believer is called not to participate in mockery, and to recognize that when God withdraws, even speech becomes foreign.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah, son of Shelah
H3935.detail: Laedan is a minor character in the genealogy of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible. He belongs to the direct lineage of Judah and represents a genealogical line extending from Shelah (his father) to Mareshah (his son). His name means "order" and marks a link in the genealogical chain of the people of Judah.
H3935.origine: The name Laedan comes from Hebrew and literally means "order." It belongs to a genealogy established during the Egyptian and desert period. The character is primarily just a name in a genealogical list intended to show the continuity of Judah's lineage through the ages.
H3935.emploi: Laedan is mentioned only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 4:21. He appears in the genealogy of Judah, presented as the son of Shelah and the father of Mareshah. This verse also places his name in the context of families distinguished by the production of fine linen, indicating the economic and professional importance of his household.

sens: Name of an Ephraimite, ancestor of Joshua
H3936G.detail: Laedan is a character from the Old Testament, a member of the tribe of Ephraim. He is mentioned as one of the ancestors of Joshua, son of Nun, who became the great leader of Israel after Moses (1 Chronicles 7:26).
H3936G.origine: The name Laedan means "put in order" or "ordered," probably referring to order or organization. It is a Hebrew name borne by at least two distinct characters in the Old Testament: this Ephraimite and a Levite of the same name, son of Gershom, also called Libni.
H3936G.emploi: Laedan is mentioned only once in the genealogy of Ephraim preserved in 1 Chronicles 7:26. This genealogy traces the descent of the sons of Joseph down to Joshua, thus establishing the genealogical link between the tribe of Ephraim and its most illustrious military and religious leader. His appearance in this genealogical list underscores the importance of family records for the people of Israel.
H3936G.portee: This passage reminds us that the leaders of the Old Testament, like Joshua, did not arise from one generation to the next: they come from established and known lineages. For the reader, this shows that God works through the history of families and that the responsibilities of God's people are passed down in a visible and verifiable human continuity.

sens: Levite son of Gershom, head of a Levitical family
H3936H.detail: Laedan is a Levite belonging to the branch of the Gershonites (descendants of Gershom, son of Levi). He appears in the genealogical register of Levitical families established by King David for the organization of the temple. His sons, including Jehiel, Zetham, and Joel, are mentioned as heads of paternal houses responsible for the service of the sanctuary (1 Chronicles 23:7-8). His name also appears among the Gershonites in charge of the temple guard and its treasures (1 Chronicles 26:21).
H3936H.origine: The name Laedan means "put in order" or "arranged" (from the idea of setting up, ordering). It is borne by this Levite who plays a role of order and organization in the structure of temple worship: his existence and that of his descendants mark the orderly continuity of Levitical priestly families.
H3936H.emploi: Laedan appears four times in the text of 1 Chronicles, exclusively in chapters 23 and 26, in the context of the census and organization of the Levites undertaken by David. He is named as the son of Gershom, father of family heads (Jehiel, Zetham, Joel), and as an ancestor of the Gershonites who had specific responsibilities in the service of the temple and the guarding of its goods. The passages emphasize his role as a head of a paternal house within the tribe of Levi.

sens: Speak a language that one does not understand or master
Pronounce confused or unintelligible words
Emit strange or barbaric sounds
H3937.detail:
1. The word primarily describes someone who speaks a different language, incomprehensible to the listener. In Psalms 114:1, when Israel leaves Egypt, the Egyptians speak a 'barbaric' language — not bad in itself, but simply foreign and unintelligible to the Israelites.
2. More generally, it refers to speaking in a confused or indistinct manner, without clarity, like someone who mumbles or stutters. The idea is of sounds that do not form comprehensible words.
3. By extension, it is to emit bizarre or foreign noises, anything that sounds 'barbaric' to the ear of the listener — the linguistic unknown that disconcerts.
H3937.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that imitates unintelligible noise: that of a foreign language or a confused word. In Hebrew, the word 'laz' or 'laz' naturally evokes the idea of babbling or incomprehensible murmuring. This root primarily expresses an auditory sensation — what does not sound clear, what is obscure to the ear.
H3937.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Bible (in Psalms 114:1), to describe the language of the Egyptians from the perspective of the Israelites: a barbaric language, that is, foreign and incomprehensible. It is a rare, almost poetic word that emphasizes the contrast between the people of Israel and those around them. The Segond translates the word as 'barbaric', which captures well this idea of linguistic and cultural strangeness.
H3937.portee: This word reminds us that the diversity of languages marked the people of God from its inception. For the believer, it evokes the experience of dislocation or incomprehension in the face of the other, and how God guides His people even amidst languages and cultures that are foreign to them. It is also an invitation to see in the Babel of languages not a permanent curse, but the context of faith and deliverance.

sens: Swallow hastily, devour without restraint
Eat eagerly, without waiting
H3938.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of swallowing greedily, of devouring. It is to eat quickly and voraciously, like someone who is very hungry. In Genesis 25:30, Esau says to Jacob: 'Let me swallow some of that red stew', meaning he wants to gulp down the red stew he urgently needs without waiting.
2. The word also evokes impatience and greed in the face of desire. Esau does not ask to eat decently or politely: he expresses his raw, immediate craving, that of a man exhausted who wants to quickly ingest.
H3938.origine: The Hebrew root לעט (la.at) carries the idea of devouring or swallowing hastily. The verb is used here in the intensive form (Hiphil), which reinforces the voracious and unrestrained nature of the action. This form emphasizes that one swallows not only quickly but greedily, with a sort of frenzy.
H3938.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Genesis 25:30. It is Esau, returning from the hunt, hungry and exhausted, who uses it to ask his brother Jacob for the red stew he has prepared. The context reveals the urgency and greed of the character: Esau does not reason, he does not evaluate the stakes (his birthright), he just wants to swallow. It is a word that paints the impulsive and carnal character of the person.
H3938.portee: This word illustrates how carnal greed and impatience can cause us to lose sight of what truly matters. Esau swallows — literally — and sells his birthright. The verb makes visible the precariousness of our choices when we allow our immediate desires to dominate us without considering the lasting consequences.

sens: Bitter and toxic plant
Extreme bitterness and pain
Poison or moral malice
Bitter consequence of sin or injustice
H3939.detail:
1. Wormwood is a real, bitter, and potentially toxic plant that the Bible mentions for its unpleasant taste and harmful effects. It symbolizes everything that is bitter to swallow or endure (Lamentations 3:15: 'He has filled me with bitterness, He has made me drunk with wormwood').
2. The word also denotes bitterness itself, not in the sense of taste, but of moral and spiritual suffering. It is the deep pain caused by misfortune or sorrow.
3. Wormwood also becomes an image of moral poison: injustice, wickedness, or false teachings that contaminate a community. Jeremiah 23:15 speaks of false prophets fed with wormwood, an image of their spiritual corruption.
4. Finally, it represents the bitter consequence of sin or divine judgment. God 'feeds' His unfaithful people with wormwood (Jeremiah 9:15), as punishment: it is a misfortune that God imposes to punish apostasy.
H3939.origine: The Hebrew word לַעֲנָה likely comes from a root expressing bitterness. Wormwood (Artemisia absinthium) was well known in the Middle East as a medicinal plant, but bitter and sometimes dangerous. The Bible first uses it in a concrete botanical sense, then transforms it into a symbol of everything that is bitter, toxic, or painful, particularly in the context of divine justice and judgment.
H3939.emploi: The word appears 8 times, concentrated in the prophetic and poetic books: Deuteronomy, Proverbs, Jeremiah, Lamentations, and Amos. In Deuteronomy 29:18, it symbolizes the sin that corrupts the people. In Proverbs 5:4, it describes the final bitterness of adultery. In Jeremiah 9:15 and 23:15, God makes His people or the false prophets 'eat wormwood': an image of punishment and imposed bitterness. In Lamentations 3:15 and 3:19, the prophet expresses his personal suffering through this image. The meaning oscillates between the botanical reality and the symbol of misfortune or perversion.
H3939.portee: Wormwood reminds us that sin and unfaithfulness inevitably lead to bitter consequences. It invites the reader to recognize the bitter taste of divine judgment and to measure the spiritual cost of distancing from God. It is also a warning: what seems attractive can turn out to be bitter and poisoned.

sens: Portable torch or lamp producing bright light
Bright fire or flame that bursts forth or burns
Object or phenomenon that shines with intense brightness
Image of that which illuminates, guides, or signals
H3940.detail:
1. A torch is a handheld light source made of flammable material fixed to the end of a stick to illuminate or signal. In Judges 7:16, Gideon gives torches to his men, hidden in jars, to create a surprise effect in battle. It is a concrete object, an instrument of lighting.
2. The word also refers to the bright flames that burst forth from an intense fire. In Job 41:10, flames come out of the mouth of Leviathan; in Ezekiel 1:13, the heavenly creatures resemble burning coals, living torches that sparkle.
3. By extension, torch describes anything that shines with a powerful and moving brightness. In Nahum 2:5, the war chariots "resemble torches" as they rush quickly and shine in the night.
4. The word takes on a symbolic meaning: that which illuminates, guides, or manifests the presence of God. In Zechariah 12:6, Jerusalem becomes "like a burning torch," an image of its light and regained strength.
H3940.origine: The Hebrew word לַפִּיד (lapid) comes from a root that evokes brightness and vivid light. It literally designates an object that produces a visible and bright flame. The family of the word includes the idea of that which rises, shines, or consumes while illuminating. This term regularly appears in the prophetic and warrior passages of the Bible, where light symbolizes strength, revelation, or the action of God.
H3940.emploi: The word lapid appears 12 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, mainly in the historical (Judges), poetic (Job, Isaiah), and prophetic (Ezekiel, Nahum, Zechariah) books. In Judges 7 and 15, it refers to actual torches, instruments of war or signaling. In Job 41 and Ezekiel 1, the word rises to the symbolic: it depicts manifestations of the divine, heavenly creatures, and phenomena that reveal invisible power. In Genesis 15:17, the smoking torch that passes between the divided animals is the sign of God's covenant with Abraham. The meaning varies little: it is always an intense light, concrete or metaphorical.
H3940.portee: The torch reminds the reader that light has power: it clarifies, signals, and protects. It is also the biblical image of divine revelation — God manifesting visibly and brilliantly, guiding His people like a light in darkness. Meditating on this word invites us to see in God the one who illuminates our path and gives us the ability to shine for Him in the world.

sens: Husband of Deborah the prophetess
H3941.detail: Lappidoth is the husband of Deborah, the prophetess and judge of Israel during the time of the Judges. He appears only once in the Bible, simply mentioned as being married to this remarkable woman who led the people of Israel and rendered justice (Judges 4:4). His name literally means "torches," which can evoke light or guidance, but he remains a discreet figure in biblical history.
H3941.origine: The name Lappidoth comes from the Hebrew לפיד (lapid), which means "torch" or "flame." The plural form evokes multiple torches, an image of light. It is a meaningful name, common in ancient Israel, but little known in the Bible since it appears only once.
H3941.emploi: Lappidoth is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Judges 4:4, where he is presented as Deborah's husband. At that time of the Judges, Deborah was herself a prophetess and judge: she was the one who led Israel and rendered judgments. The text provides no details about Lappidoth himself, no actions he may have taken. He remains in the background, identified only by his marital connection to this woman of power and wisdom.
H3941.portee: The mention of Lappidoth reminds us that great servants of God also have family lives, and that sometimes God places His gifts of leadership and prophecy on a woman, while her husband remains in a more modest position. This shows the importance of supporting those whom God calls, regardless of the context.

sens: To take firmly in one's arms or hands, with some energy
To lean, to turn towards something or someone
To deviate, to stray from one's path
H3943.detail:
1. The verb primarily describes the action of seizing something solidly, often with the arms. Samson "embraces" the two pillars of the temple to shake them (Judges 16:29): he surrounds and grips them with his strength to make them fall.
2. It can also mean to lean, that is, to incline one's body towards someone or something. The man from Bethlehem "leans" in the night to look at Ruth lying at his feet (Ruth 3:8), a tender and attentive gesture.
3. In a figurative sense, the word takes on a shade of diversion or deviation: the caravans deviate from their path and plunge into the desert (Job 6:18), changing direction, straying from the safe road.
H3943.origine: The Hebrew word lafat comes from a root that evokes the idea of twisting, turning, bending. This image of twisting or turning underlies all its uses: one twists their body to seize, one bends to lean, one diverts or deviates from their path. The root expresses the circular or winding movement of the body or a trajectory.
H3943.emploi: The verb lafat appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Judges 16:29, it describes the physical and powerful gesture of Samson embracing the pillars. In Ruth 3:8, it describes the tender movement of the Redeemer leaning to see Ruth. In Job 6:18, it takes on a more abstract meaning: the caravans deviate from their path and perish. The word remains concrete, anchored in bodily gestures or images of movement, but its range goes from the gesture of embrace to the diversion of the path.
H3943.portee: This word reminds us that to seize is to lean towards the other, to seek contact and closeness. Samson seizes by force; the man from Bethlehem leans out of tenderness; the caravans deviate out of waywardness. Each use invites reflection on the meaning of the gesture: strength is not always beneficial, closeness can be an act of love, and straying from the path can be fatal.

sens: attitude of one who mocks, ridicules
words or behavior showing contempt towards someone or something
arrogant confidence in one's own superiority
H3944.detail: 1. Mockery is primarily the attitude of the mocker, one who takes pleasure in ridiculing. In Proverbs 1:22, the text describes the foolish who love foolishness and the mockers who love mockery: it is the pleasure taken in deriding, in despising. 2. It is also the mocking word or action itself, the contempt expressed. In Proverbs 29:8, the mockers "blow fire" in the city by spreading their derision, which disturbs the peace. 3. By extension, it is a presumptuous arrogance, a carnal confidence in one's own greatness. In Isaiah 28:14, the prophet addresses the "mockers" who dominate in Jerusalem: their mockery is also a proud challenge to the word of God.
H3944.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of deriding, of being clever. It is related to the verb that means to mock, ridicule. This vocabulary of mockery evokes the arrogance of one who believes themselves smarter than others and despises them.
H3944.emploi: The word appears three times in the Old Testament, first in Proverbs, which repeat it to characterize a type of person: the mocker, the fool who loves mockery more than wisdom. In Proverbs 1:22, it describes the mocker's love for their own derision; in Proverbs 29:8, this mocking spirit has devastating social effects. Isaiah uses it differently: it is the prophet who calls the political leaders mockers who arrogantly reject the divine word. The meaning nuances: from the personal attitude of the derider to the collective arrogance of power that defies God.
H3944.portee: Mockery is presented in the Bible as a form of moral and spiritual folly. It closes the heart to wisdom and to God, it disturbs communal peace, and it ultimately attracts judgment. The Christian must recognize it within themselves and turn away from it: not to laugh with the mockers, but to seek wisdom and humility in the face of the divine word.

sens: fortified city in the territory of Naphtali, on the northern border
H3946.detail: 1. Lakkum is a fortified city, a geographical landmark located on the northern border of the territory assigned to the tribe of Naphtali during the distribution of the Promised Land. It marks a point in the delineation of this boundary, between Adami-Nekeb and Jabneel, near the Jordan (Joshua 19:33).
H3946.origine: The Hebrew name לַקּוּם (Lakkum) means "fortification" or "stronghold." It comes from a root that evokes the construction or solidity of a defensive structure. This name reflects the strategic importance of this territorial anchor point in the north of the land of Israel.
H3946.emploi: Lakkum appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:33, where the cities and geographical points delineating the territory of Naphtali are listed. It is included in this list as a point of the northeastern border of the tribe, illustrating the rigor with which the Torah describes the division of the land among the twelve tribes. Its precise location remains to be archaeologically identified in the current Palestinian terrain.

sens: to grasp with the hand, to seize something
to take away, to remove, to withdraw from
to receive, to welcome, to accept
to choose, to select for oneself
to lead, to bring, to cause to come
to undergo, to be the object of (in the passive form)
H3947G.detail:
1. To grasp with the hand, to seize something: the physical and concrete action of putting one's hand on an object or a person to have it in one's possession. This is the simplest and most common meaning. Example: Moses "took" the stone tablets from Sinai, Aaron "took" the censer (Numbers 16:47).
2. To take away, to remove from: to take something from someone, to snatch or subtract it from a place. This includes the idea of separation or deprivation. Example: the ark of God was "taken" by the Philistines (1 Samuel 4:17), or Isaiah says that the people were "taken" away for nothing (Isaiah 52:5).
3. To receive, to welcome, to accept: voluntary acceptance of what is offered, a proposal, or a person. This is to take with consent. Example: Abimelech "received" Hagar as a wife (Genesis 16:3).
4. To choose, to select for oneself: to take something or someone from among others for a particular action or purpose. Example: Noah "took" from every kind of clean animals (Genesis 7:2) to put them in the ark.
5. To lead, to bring, to cause to come: to take someone or something to bring him/her/it elsewhere. Example: the Lord "took" Adam and "placed" him in the garden of Eden (Genesis 2:15).
6. To undergo, to be the object of (in the passive form): to be taken, captured, removed against one's will. This is the reverse of the active action: to be seized or conquered.
H3947G.origine: The Hebrew verb לָקַח comes from a root that evokes the action of seizing, holding firmly. The base form expresses the simple gesture of taking in hand. Different nuances (Qal, Niphal, Pual, Hophal) show the same act viewed from different angles: actively taking, being taken, or being led to take. It is an extremely common verb in the Bible, appearing more than 700 times; it conveys the fundamental idea of acquisition, seizing, and possession.
H3947G.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Old Testament (733 occurrences) and appears in all the books. It designates very varied acts: taking bread (Genesis 3:6), taking a wife (Genesis 3:22), taking a road, taking a weapon to fight, taking vengeance, or being taken captive. In Genesis, it expresses the action of seizing, choosing, welcoming: Adam "takes" the woman, Noah "takes" the animals, Abraham "takes" Hagar. Its fundamental meaning remains physical and concrete, but it easily extends to a figurative sense: to make a decision, to take courage, "to take heed." In passages of captivity or loss, it changes perspective (passive form): being "taken" means being defeated or carried away.
H3947G.portee: Understanding this verb helps the reader perceive how the Bible values concrete action, will, and responsibility: one "takes" what one desires, one "is taken" when defeated. It also reminds us that God "takes" man and "places" him (Genesis 2:15)—an image of protection and divine order. The verb invites reflection on what we grasp and what we refuse, and on the difference between acting freely and being taken or dominated by circumstances.

sens: To grasp something with the hand or to carry it
To take away, to remove from someone
To receive something that is offered or presented to you
To welcome, to accept a word, a teaching, a counsel
To choose, to select someone or something
To capture, to seize by force
H3947H.detail:
1. To grasp something with the hand or to carry it: this is the simplest and most common meaning. One takes an object to hold it or transport it from one place to another. Numbers 7:5 illustrates this: the command to "take" the offerings for use in the sanctuary.
2. To take away, to remove from someone: to take here carries a nuance of appropriation or subtraction. It is to deprive someone of what they possess. In Genesis 4:11, the earth "receives" the blood of the murder — it takes it, receives it from a murderous hand.
3. To receive something that is offered or presented to you: to accept a gift, a present, a proposal. In 2 Kings 5:15, Naaman asks Elisha to "accept" a gift, meaning to receive it as a sign of gratitude.
4. To welcome, to accept a word, a teaching, a counsel: to take in the sense of internalizing, to receive favorably in one's heart what is taught to us. Proverbs 21:11 shows the wise man who "welcomes" knowledge — he receives and absorbs it.
5. To choose, to select someone or something: to deliberately decide to take someone for a particular function or role. Proverbs 1:3 and nearby contexts illustrate this in the choice of a path or wisdom.
6. To capture, to seize by force: in a military sense or in a relationship of domination. Psalms 49:16 uses "take" to express that God will save the soul from the grave — he will take it back under his authority.
H3947H.origine: The verb לָקַח (laqach) is a fundamental Hebrew root whose primary image is that of the hand grasping. It has no known etymology beyond Hebrew itself. This verb has generated many grammatical forms (Qal, Niphal, Pual, Hophal, Hithpael) that slightly affect the meaning: in the simple form (Qal), one actively takes; in the passive form, one is taken or received. It is one of the most frequent verbs in the Hebrew lexicon, used to express almost any act of appropriation or reception.
H3947H.emploi: This verb appears 72 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, and Psalms. It is first used in a concrete sense: to take an object, an offering, a ransom (Exodus 25:2-3, Numbers 31:51-54). It then extends to the legal and moral domain: to receive a ransom (Numbers 35:31-32), to accept a gift (Deuteronomy 16:19, 2 Kings 5:15-26). It also applies to the reception of the divine word or teaching: "to receive" instruction, wisdom, correction (Proverbs 2:1, 9:7, Jeremiah 35:13). Finally, it describes God's salvific action, who "takes" or "recovers" a soul (Psalms 49:16, 68:19), expressing protection and deliverance.
H3947H.portee: This word reminds the believer that everything comes from God and that life consists of receiving his gifts and his word. To take also means to voluntarily receive, with gratitude, what is presented to us — a central attitude in faith. Conversely, refusing to "take" God's word or teachings is to close oneself off from his will and wisdom. Ultimately, the image of God who "takes" our souls expresses his protective sovereignty and our trust in him.

sens: Son of Shemida, grandson of Manasseh, of the tribe of Manasseh
H3949.detail: Likchi is a man of the tribe of Manasseh mentioned only once in the Old Testament. He is the son of Shemida and the brother of Ahian, Shechem, and Aniam. His name appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Manasseh, a record that lists the families and lineages of the people of Israel.
H3949.origine: The name Likchi means "learning" or "one who learns." It comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of receiving or acquiring knowledge. This name reflects an important value in Israelite culture: knowledge and the transmission of teaching within families.
H3949.emploi: Likchi appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:19, in the heart of the genealogy of the tribe of Manasseh. He is listed among the four sons of Shemida, alongside his brothers. His inclusion in this genealogical record shows his importance in the eyes of the historical writers as a link in the genealogical chain of the people of Israel.

sens: To take and gather scattered objects from the ground
To glean the leftover ears or fruits after the harvest
To collect, to gather into a heap or collection
To gather one's strength or recover
H3950.detail:
1. To take and gather scattered objects: this is the concrete action of picking up what is lying around. Jacob tells his brothers: "Gather stones" to make a heap (Genesis 31:46). The Israelites in the desert gather the manna that falls from heaven, some more, some less (Exodus 16:17).
2. To glean the leftover ears or fruits: gleaning is to follow the harvest to pick up the ears forgotten in the field. Ruth goes to glean in Boaz's field and finds favor in his eyes (Ruth 2:8, 2:19). The Law commands to leave for gleaning for the poor and the foreigners (Leviticus 19:9-10).
3. To collect, to gather: the word also describes the action of gathering various things into a heap or collection, like Joseph who collects grain in Egypt (Genesis 47:14).
4. To gather one's strength: in a figurative sense, it means to regain courage or recover, like someone who gathers themselves together to act.
H3950.origine: The Hebrew root laqat evokes the simple and repeated action of taking, picking, gathering what is accessible. It is an active and concrete word, related to the work of hands and sustenance. The word belongs to the vocabulary of daily and agricultural life in ancient Israel. It expresses both human action and the gesture of God who "gathers" or provides (Psalm 104:28).
H3950.emploi: The verb laqat appears 34 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the narratives of the Exodus (the manna), the book of Ruth (the harvest and gleaning), and the laws of Leviticus. Its most common usage is "to gather" (17 times) and "to glean" (11 times). In Exodus, it describes the collection of the manna by the Israelites in the desert (Exodus 16:17, 16:27). In Ruth, it refers to gleaning: Ruth gathers the ears after the harvesters (Ruth 2:7, 2:8, 2:17), and Boaz encourages her to stay in his field. Leviticus prescribes leaving for the poor to glean (Leviticus 19:9-10). The word is also used in the sense of gathering or collecting (like money in Genesis 47:14) and even figuratively to express a reduction or weakening (Judges 1:7).
H3950.portee: This word reminds us that God provides for the needs of the poor and the foreigners, not through humiliating charity but by allowing them to glean. It also teaches economy: each one gathers what they can, according to their strength. Ruth, a widow and foreigner, gleaning with humility, becomes a model of dignity and honest work. For the believer, gathering speaks of receiving God's blessings and collecting within oneself what builds up.

sens: what remains after the main harvest
what the harvester intentionally leaves in the field
the portion designated for the poor and the foreigners
H3951.detail:
1. The word refers to the ears or sheaves forgotten or left after the field has been harvested. It is the product that the harvesters do not collect — either by oversight or deliberately. In Leviticus 19:9, the law commands the owner not to complete their harvest: they must leave a corner of the field unharvested, thus leaving a "remainder" for gleaning.
2. This remainder becomes a provision for the poor and the foreigners. The law in Leviticus 23:22 specifies that the owner "shall leave it for the poor and the foreigner," establishing a moral obligation: the remainder of the harvest is not an optional charity, but a right guaranteed to the most vulnerable in the community.
H3951.origine: The Hebrew word לֶקֶט (leqet) comes from a root meaning "to gather" or "to pick up." It evokes the action of gathering the scattered ears on the ground after the passage of the harvesters. It is a very concrete term, related to daily agricultural work, which has come to specifically designate the leftovers left for the poor — a fundamental practice in the law of Moses.
H3951.emploi: The word appears twice in the Segond, in the two places where the Torah states the same law regarding the harvests: Leviticus 19:9 and 23:22. These two verses outline the instruction that the owner of a field must respect: not to harvest down to the last ear, but to intentionally leave a remainder so that the needy can glean for free. The remainder of the harvest illustrates a fundamental social principle of the Old Testament: providing for the needs of the poor and the foreigners through an implicit sharing of the fruits of the land.
H3951.portee: This law teaches the believer a form of structural generosity: it is not just about occasional alms, but an obligation integrated into the work itself. By recognizing that the poor have a right to the remainder of the harvest, the Bible reminds us that work and property have a communal dimension. For the Christian, this reveals the heart of God who provides for all, especially the vulnerable, and inspires a stewardship of resources that is not selfish.

sens: To drink by bringing the liquid to the mouth with the tongue
To lick a surface with the tongue
H3952.detail:
1. To lap is to drink by lapping like an animal: one brings the tongue to the liquid and absorbs it quickly, without bending down, often using one's hand. This is the sense of the word in the story of Gideon (Judges 7:5-7), where the soldiers who lap water with their hand brought to their mouth are separated from the others, and this detail becomes miraculous: with these three hundred men only, the Lord promises to give victory over the Midianites.
2. To lick means to pass one's tongue over a surface to clean it or to absorb what is there. In the accounts of the punishment of Ahab (1 Kings 21:19 and 22:38), the dogs lick the spilled blood: this is the terrible fulfillment of the prophetic word of divine judgment.
H3952.origine: The Hebrew word לָקַק (laqaq) imitates the sound and gesture: it is an onomatopoeia that evokes the sound of a tongue lapping or licking. The root is very ancient and common to several Semitic languages. It expresses a simple and animal act: to absorb a liquid or to clean a surface with the tongue.
H3952.emploi: The verb appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always in a concrete and immediate sense. Three occurrences are found in the account of the selection of Gideon's soldiers (Judges 7:5-7), where "lapping" becomes a miraculous criterion of divine selection: those who lap water while remaining vigilant and bringing their hand to their mouth, rather than kneeling down to drink, are the three hundred men through whom God will achieve victory. The other two occurrences (1 Kings 21:19 and 22:38) refer to the dogs licking Ahab's blood, fulfilling the prophetic sentence. The word never strays from its physical meaning: it describes observable acts.
H3952.portee: This simple and vivid word enriches the account of Gideon's selection by showing how the Lord acts through concrete details: the manner of drinking reveals the character and vigilance of the warrior. It also reminds us that divine judgment is fulfilled even in its smallest details, as when the dogs lick the blood of the wicked king, confirming the certainty of the prophetic word.

sens: To collect the ears or forgotten fruits after the harvest
To gather the leftovers, what escaped the main harvest
To strip someone of everything they own
H3953.detail:
1. Gleaning primarily means to go and gather after the harvest: to pick up the ears of grain or grapes that have been left in the fields or vineyards, what the workers have missed. It is a humble task but regulated by law: the poor had the right to glean (Leviticus 19:9). In Job 24:6, the unfortunate glean in the vineyard of the wicked, seeking something to survive.
2. The word extends to the sense of collecting the remnants of something, the abandoned crumbs — literally or figuratively, anything that remains after others have taken their share.
3. In the intensive form (Piel), gleaning takes on a destructive sense: it means to strip someone, to take everything they possess, leaving nothing, completely stripping them — just as one removes even the last fruits from a ravaged vineyard.
H3953.origine: The Hebrew verb laqash belongs to a root that expresses the idea of gathering or seizing. The word translates the well-known activity of gleaning, an ancient and Eastern practice: after the main harvest, one would return to glean the leftovers. The root evokes the action of picking up small items, taking what remains, what is lying around. In biblical Hebrew, it is a rare but concrete verb.
H3953.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Bible: in Job 24:6. The context shows Job describing the misery of the poor: they must glean — gather the leftovers — in the vineyards of the wicked to survive. It is a picture of extreme poverty: the unfortunate have no other resource than to seek what has been forgotten or left behind. The word emphasizes both the humility of this work and social injustice: these people are reduced to gleaning while others hoard the harvests.
H3953.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not turn a blind eye to misery. It acknowledges the existence of those who live off the leftovers, and it grants them dignity and rights — the law allowed gleaning. For the believer, it is an invitation to see the poor and to respect the divine order of social justice: to leave something for the weak, not to hoard everything.

sens: grass or young crop that sprouts after the first harvest
the time of year when this regrowth appears
new growth, a restart after a pause
H3954.detail:
1. Regrowth is the grass or grains that naturally sprout after the first harvest has been reaped. In Amos 7:1, the prophet sees in a vision locusts formed "at the time when the regrowth began to grow," that is, in spring, when after the royal harvest, new vegetation emerges from the ground.
2. This word also designates the time of year corresponding to this regrowth, a season of hope and renewal: it is "after the king's cutting" that the regrowth appears.
3. By extension, regrowth evokes any form of restarting or new growth after an interruption, making it a powerful image of restoration or recovery.
H3954.origine: The Hebrew word לקש (leqesh) comes from a root that means "to be late" or "that comes after." It specifically designates this grass or crop that emerges late, after the first harvest, as a natural cycle of renewal. It is a concrete word rooted in the agricultural life of the Middle East.
H3954.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in the prophetic vision of Amos. The prophet receives a divine vision showing locusts forming at the time of regrowth — this temporal detail is not insignificant: it is precisely when the earth begins to regenerate that a threat of destruction arises. This image contrasts the fragility of the restart with the peril that threatens it.
H3954.portee: For the Christian reader, this image of regrowth reminds us that every restart, every restoration after a trial is fragile and under God's watch. It invites us to recognize that survival and recovery do not depend solely on our own strength, but on divine grace.

sens: food preparation baked from flour and oil
dryness, aridity of the body or soul
H3955.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a pastry or culinary preparation. In Numbers 11:8, the Israelites in the desert gather the manna, grind it, cook it in a pot, and make cakes from it, showing that it is a worked and enjoyed food, rich and thick like a crafted dish.
2. The word is also used figuratively to describe the state of an exhausted body or a dried-up spirit. In Psalms 32:4, the psalmist says that his strength is nothing but dryness (the same word in Hebrew): he uses the image of a dry cake, without moisture, to express the weakening and depression caused by guilt before confession.
H3955.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of fatness, richness, abundance. It relates לָשָׁד to other words describing prosperity and fertility. In neighboring ancient Semitic languages, the word retains this sense of rich and nourishing food, linked to oil and fat that characterize a delicious dish.
H3955.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. It first designates a culinary preparation made from the manna in the desert (Numbers 11:8), showing how the Israelites transformed this heavenly food into tasty dishes. Then it takes on a metaphorical value in Psalms 32:4, where the body of the penitent becomes as dry as a dried cake, an image of the inner dryness caused by the weight of unconfessed sin. These two uses explore two opposing aspects: richness and abundance on one side, deprivation and exhaustion on the other.
H3955.portee: This word helps the reader understand two truths: first, that the Bible takes our sensory joys and foods seriously, as it speaks of food with flavor and pleasure. Secondly, it speaks of sin as a kind of inner dryness, a loss of vital moisture, energy, and joy — which shows that confessing one's sins is a return to life and abundance.

sens: The physical organ in the mouth that allows for speaking and tasting
The words that a person utters; what they say
The language of a people, their way of communicating
The tongue of fire, an elongated flame
An elongated and narrow form
H3956G.detail:
1. The tongue is primarily the physical organ: Exodus 4:10 shows Moses complaining of having "a heavy tongue," meaning a defect that makes speaking difficult. It is the concrete instrument of speech.

2. By natural extension, the word also refers to the words themselves: in Psalms 10:7, "under his tongue" there is "malice and iniquity," meaning that this person utters wicked words. The tongue represents what comes out of the mouth.

3. The term also evokes the language of a people, their mother tongue: Isaiah 33:19 speaks of peoples whose "language" will not be understood. It is the dialect or way of speaking of a community.

4. Isaiah 30:27 mentions "the tongue of his fire," an image where the tongue signifies a fiery form that rises and consumes.

5. Due to its narrowness and elongated shape, the tongue can also refer to a narrow strip of land or a maritime bay (less common meaning in the provided texts).
H3956G.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root that primarily describes the organ of the body. Its first image — that which is elongated, narrow, and pointed — explains why it also denotes a tongue of fire, a tongue of land. By moving from the physical (the organ) to the functional (what is said), and then to the abstract (the tongue as the language of a people), the Hebrew word shows how the Bible views the tongue: not only as a member of the body but especially as the instrument of the power of words.
H3956G.emploi: This word appears 93 times in the provided Old Testament, mostly in Psalms and Proverbs, where it concerns the power of words: a tongue that lies (Proverbs 21:6), that wounds (Proverbs 12:18), that soothes (Proverbs 15:4), or that praises God (Psalms 35:28). Job also mentions the tongue in his sufferings (Job 6:30). Isaiah uses it to speak of God's judgment: "his tongue" burns like fire (Isaiah 30:27). The context shows that the Bible considers the tongue as the seat of a person's moral character: it reveals who we truly are.
H3956G.portee: The Bible emphasizes the weight of the tongue: it can kill or give life (Proverbs 18:21). Recognizing that our words come from our tongue — and thus from our heart — calls us to vigilance. Psalms and Proverbs teach us to keep our tongue from evil, to master it. This entry helps the believer understand that speech is never neutral: it expresses who we are and shapes those who listen.

sens: The physical organ in the mouth that allows for speaking and tasting
The system of words and sounds that a nation or people uses to communicate
A particular way of expressing oneself or a dialect specific to a group
The power of speech, considered morally or spiritually
H3956H.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the physical tongue, the organ of the human body that serves two essential functions: speech and taste. This is the most concrete and direct meaning.

2. By extension, it signifies the spoken language — that is, the system of words, the way of communicating that a people uses. In Genesis 10:5, it speaks of nations that separate according to their "language," meaning according to their own way of speaking, the linguistic code that distinguishes them from others. This is the most common meaning in the provided usages.

3. The word can also refer to a tongue as a dialect or specific register: in Nehemiah 13:24, some did not know how to speak "the language" of the Jewish people, meaning Hebrew with its pronunciation and specific turns of phrase.

4. Finally, in a figurative sense, the "tongue" can represent the power of moral or spiritual speech — the ability to bless or curse, to instruct or mislead. This dimension appears in the Psalms, where one asks God to divide the tongues of enemies (Psalms 55:10), meaning to destroy their ability to communicate and understand each other.
H3956H.origine: The Hebrew word לָשׁוֹן (lashon) refers to the organ of speech and likely comes from an ancient root related to the idea of "pulling" or "stretching" — the tongue indeed stretches and moves when one speaks. The same root has given rise to other Hebrew words designating that which extends or projects. The word has naturally extended to denote any language or communication system of a people, as if saying "the language of the Assyrians" to mean "the way the Assyrians speak." This progression from the physical to the abstract meaning is very typical in Hebrew.
H3956H.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the sense of "spoken language" or "speech." It is common in the accounts of the dispersion of peoples (Genesis 10) and in the books concerning empires (Isaiah, Daniel, Ezra-Nehemiah), where the existence of many languages is mentioned as a reality of the divine world. In Esther, the king orders that his edicts be written "according to the language" of each people, showing that each nation has its own language and that political power must take this into account. In Isaiah 66:18, God gathers "all nations and all languages" to see His glory, giving the word an eschatological and missionary significance. The word also figuratively and morally designates human speech as power: to divide the tongues (Psalms 55:10) means to break the understanding between enemies. Nowhere does the word denote a language in the sense of literature or accumulated knowledge.
H3956H.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that the diversity of languages is willed by God and marks human history. It is not a punishment to be rid of, but a reality that God respects and that the Gospel traverses: the disciples of Christ receive the ability to speak in other languages (Acts 2) so that everyone hears in their own language. Meditating on the "tongue" also invites reflection on the power of speech: what we say, the languages we use, shape the world and testify to our hearts. Mastery of speech is therefore a central moral and spiritual issue.

sens: The organ of the mouth that allows for speaking and tasting
Language, the ability to express oneself
An elongated and narrow form that extends, like a tongue
H3956I.detail:
1. The tongue is primarily the physical organ in the mouth, which allows humans to speak and communicate. This is the most direct meaning of the word.
2. The word also refers to the tongue in the sense of language or speech — the way in which one expresses and communicates ideas. This is a natural extension of the role of the organ that produces speech.
3. By resemblance of shape, the word describes any narrow and elongated prominence that extends: a coastal bay, a tongue of land that juts into the sea (Joshua 15:2), or even an elongated gold ingot (Joshua 7:21). The word emphasizes the characteristic silhouette — pointed and stretched.
H3956I.origine: The Hebrew word לָשׁוֹן comes from a root that designates the organ of the mouth. This elongated and mobile form has naturally given its name to anything that presents a similar shape: a bay that extends into the sea resembles a tongue coming out of the mouth. In Hebrew, this type of visual resemblance forms the basis for many concrete names.
H3956I.emploi: The word appears six times in the provided usages. Four times, it refers to a tongue of land or a coastal bay that extends into the Salt Sea and the Jordan (Joshua 15:2, 15:5, 18:19, Isaiah 11:15) — this is the most frequent geographical usage in these passages. Twice, it describes an elongated gold ingot taken by Achan (Joshua 7:21, 7:24). The basic image — something that stretches and extends — remains the same: it is always the shape that prevails. The word never appears here in the sense of "speech" or "language," but always to designate a physical elongated form.
H3956I.portee: This word reminds us how the Bible views the concrete world: simple names of body objects become images to describe geography and the shapes of things. For the Christian, it is an invitation to notice how God speaks through the visible world — even a geographical detail can carry a name that awakens the imagination and makes reading the Bible more vivid.

sens: Closed room in a building, intended for living or storage
Room designated for a specific activity or function
Small room or specialized cell
Reserved or underground place
H3957.detail:
1. A chamber is primarily a closed room in a house or building where one lives or stores things. This is the simplest meaning: an interior space with walls. In 1 Samuel 9:22, Samuel brings Saul into a dining room — a chamber intended to receive guests.

2. The word also refers to a room or space assigned for a specific function. In the Temple, the chambers serve various purposes: storing offerings, housing the singers, preparing priestly garments. In Ezekiel 42:5, the upper chambers of the Temple were narrower than the lower ones — these are rooms built specifically for the needs of worship.

3. Sometimes, the word refers to cells or small specialized rooms, such as the chambers of the singers in the inner courtyard of the Temple (Ezekiel 40:44), or the chambers where the Rechabites lived according to their vow (Jeremiah 35:2).

4. In a palatial or cultic context, a chamber can be a confined place, sometimes underground or secluded, intended to preserve something or isolate someone — the word always expresses the idea of a closed and distinct space.
H3957.origine: The Hebrew word לִשְׁכָּה comes from a root that expresses the idea of being dark, closed, or confined. It is a feminine noun attested 41 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical and prophetic texts. The word primarily evokes a small, interior, and defined space. It is also found in Aramaic with a similar meaning. It is a practical and common term: it is not reserved for royal or sacred buildings but simply describes any chamber or room.
H3957.emploi: Used 41 times in the Old Testament, the word לִשְׁכָּה appears mainly in historical books (Chronicles, Nehemiah, Ezra) and prophetic books (Jeremiah, Ezekiel). It designates the chambers of the Temple — those of the singers, the priests, the storage of offerings — which frequently appear in the precise description of the restored Temple. It is also seen in domestic contexts: the chamber where one receives (1 Samuel 9:22), where one reads the prophet's word (Jeremiah 36:10), where one withdraws (Jeremiah 35:2). Ezekiel uses this word very frequently to describe the multiple chambers and galleries of his vision of the future Temple — more than ten occurrences in Ezekiel 40-46. The word does not change its fundamental meaning: it is always a closed room, but the context shows whether it is domestic, administrative, sacred, or specialized.
H3957.portee: This word reminds us that biblical life took place in defined and organized spaces — the Temple had its chambers strictly assigned to their functions, just as a house had its rooms. For the Christian, this emphasizes order, the separation of the sacred and the profane, and respect for the house of God. When Nehemiah purifies the chambers of the Temple profaned by Tobiah (Nehemiah 13:8-9), he restores divine order. This concrete word brings us closer to the material reality of worship in the Old Testament.

sens: Precious stone of bluish or greenish color
Stone of the priestly breastplate, third row
H3958.detail:
1. The opal is a hard precious stone, probably bluish or greenish in color, used in antiquity as a valuable object. It appears in the description of the high priest's breastplate, this liturgical ornament that contained twelve precious stones arranged in three rows of four.
2. In the high priest's breastplate, the opal occupies the third position of the third row, between the agate and the amethyst (Exodus 28:19; Exodus 39:12). This stone was part of the twelve stones symbolizing the twelve tribes of Israel and held major ceremonial importance.
H3958.origine: The Hebrew word לֶשֶׁם (leshem) specifically designates this precious stone; its exact etymology remains debated by scholars. The stone was known and valued in the ancient Near Eastern world. It was among the precious materials that the Egyptian people would have provided to Israel during the Exodus, resources used to build the sanctuary.
H3958.emploi: The word לֶשֶׁם (leshem) appears only twice in the Bible, both in the context of the priestly breastplate: once during the divine prescription (Exodus 28:19) and once during its actual construction (Exodus 39:12). These two passages describe exactly the same reality, confirming the importance of this stone in the official worship of Israel. It is not mentioned anywhere else in the Old Testament.
H3958.portee: The opal of the breastplate reminds us that the worship of God in Israel was expressed through beauty and preciousness, reflecting divine glory. The twelve stones represented the entirety of God's people presented before the Lord, each tribe having its distinctive place in this sacred service.

sens: City located west of Mount Hermon, formerly called Laish
City that the tribe of Dan conquered and renamed Dan
H3959.detail:
1. Léschem is a city in Canaan located west of Mount Hermon, in the northern part of the country. It has another name in the Bible: Laish. It is a stronghold that existed before the arrival of Israel.
2. The sons of Dan, after initially receiving a first territory in the south (which displeased them because it was too small and too populated with enemies), went north, conquered this city, and took it by force. They renamed it "Dan" in honor of their ancestor, the father of their tribe (Joshua 19:47). This name change marked Israel's possession of the place.
H3959.origine: The name literally means "precious stone." It is a proper name, the ancient name of the place we better know as Laish, then Dan. This name change reflects a significant historical event: the conquest of the territory by the tribe of Dan and its permanent establishment in the north of the country.
H3959.emploi: Léschem appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:47. This passage recounts the conquest of this city by the sons of Dan during the distribution of the lands after entering Canaan. Unable to fully conquer their first territory in the south, the Danites turned north and took this city. They then renamed it "Dan," a name that became very well known later in the history of Israel ("from Dan to Beersheba" became a famous expression to denote the entire land).
H3959.portee: This conquest reminds us that Israel's establishment in Canaan occurred gradually, in stages, and that the tribes had to adapt their plans and persevere in the face of obstacles. It also shows how a people establishes its presence by renaming places: it is a way of saying "this territory is ours now."

sens: Falsely or maliciously accuse someone by speaking against them
Speak ill of someone in their absence to discredit them
Defame in a way that harms another's reputation
H3960.detail:
1. Falsely or maliciously accuse someone by speaking against them: the word describes the act of launching serious and false accusations against a person. It is using words as a weapon to destroy the trust one has in someone (Proverbs 30:10).
2. Speak ill of someone in their absence to discredit them: slander differs from direct criticism; it operates in the shadows, spreading rumors or half-truths. King David refuses to tolerate one who slanders "in secret" his neighbor (Psalms 101:5).
3. Defame in a way that harms another's reputation: beyond mere words, to slander is to act with the intention of ruining a person's honor and social standing.
H3960.origine: The Hebrew word לָשַׁן comes from the root לִשְׁנָה ("tongue"), which emphasizes that it is through speech, this powerful instrument, that one slanders. The tongue (לָשׁוֹן) can thus be a source of life or destruction. This verb describes the perverted use of speech to hurt others.
H3960.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. Psalms 101:5 places it at the heart of a royal declaration on justice: the king refuses to tolerate slander, which is a serious violation of the order of the kingdom. Proverbs 30:10 uses it as a warning: one should not slander a servant, for it will provoke the servant's own curse. In both cases, slander is presented as a serious sin, incompatible with justice and the fear of God.
H3960.portee: The Bible warns severely against slander: it is a way of killing by words, innocently destroying another's honor. It is an affront to God Himself, who sees all and defends the oppressed. For the Christian, this teaches that words engage moral conscience and that one must be a guardian of their tongue, refusing to spread lies or malice.

sens: The physical organ in the mouth that allows for speaking and tasting
The system of words and language that a community uses to communicate
A group of people united by the same language
H3961.detail:
1. The tongue is primarily the organ of the body that allows for the formation of speech sounds. This is the physical and concrete sense of the word.
2. The tongue then refers to the entire set of words and rules of communication of a community — what is called a "language" in the modern sense. It distinguishes one people from another, as in the decrees of King Nebuchadnezzar that address "all peoples, nations, and men of every language" (Daniel 4:1). Each "language" represents a distinct way of speaking.
3. By extension, the "tongue" eventually designates the human group that speaks it — a set of people united by their way of communicating. Thus, "all peoples, nations, and men of every language" become almost synonymous: they are not just ways of speaking, but entire communities (Daniel 3:7, 5:19).
H3961.origine: The word comes from the root that designates the physical organ. In Hebrew, as in other languages, it is the concrete organ (the tongue in the mouth) that gave its name to speech itself, then to the spoken language, and then to the people who speak it. This progression from the concrete to the figurative is natural: what comes out of the tongue is called "tongue."
H3961.emploi: The word appears 7 times, only in the book of Daniel (chapters 3 to 7), in contexts of royal power and universal empire. The decrees of King Nebuchadnezzar and King Darius regularly address "all peoples, nations, and men of every language" who inhabit the conquered territory. In these passages, "tongue" means both the speech proper to each group and the group itself. The word appears especially in the official formulas of royal edicts, highlighting that the kingdom extends over populations speaking different idioms. In Daniel 7:14, a vision speaks of peoples and languages honoring the Son of Man.
H3961.portee: This word reminds us that God reigns over a diverse humanity, where each speaks their own language. In the royal decrees of the book of Daniel, the different languages testify to the extent of power; but they, as well as the kingdoms that speak them, are under the sovereignty of God. For the Christian, this word evokes the universality of God's plan: it is not limited to a single culture or people, but embraces all languages and all peoples.

sens: Place in Palestine located at the borders of the territory of the Canaanites
Region near Sodom and Gomorrah
H3962.detail: 1. Lesha is a locality in Palestine mentioned as a landmark of the borders of the territory of the Canaanites, alongside Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim (Genesis 10:19). It is a specific geographical location, although its exact location is uncertain today. 2. The name itself means "fissure," which could evoke a region of hills or rugged terrain. Lesha marked the southeast limit of Canaanite territory, in a region of the Jordan Valley or the southern Dead Sea.
H3962.origine: The Hebrew name לֶשַׁע comes from a root meaning "fissure" or "crevice," possibly evoking a notable geographical relief. This place is also known by the alternative name Nahaliel ("valley of God"), which reinforces the idea of a region marked by visible geological formations.
H3962.emploi: Lesha is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 10:19, in the context of the genealogical account of Noah's sons and the delineation of the borders of peoples. It appears alongside the cursed cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, indicating that this place was known as belonging to the southern region of Canaan, likely near the Dead Sea. It serves as a historical and geographical reference for understanding the extent of Canaanite settlement in ancient times.

sens: A measure of capacity for grains, particularly barley
About half a homer, or five ephahs
H3963.detail:
1. Lethec is a unit of measure used in the Old Testament to measure grains, especially barley. It is a measure of capacity, meaning volume, not weight. In Hosea 3:2, the prophet says he bought a woman "for fifteen shekels of silver, a homer of barley, and a lethec of barley": the lethec appears here as an additional quantity of barley added to the main price.
2. The lethec represents a defined quantity: it is approximately half a homer (which is itself a large measure), or the equivalent of five ephahs. This precision shows that the Israelites had an established metric system for the trade of crops and the exchange of goods.
H3963.origine: The Hebrew word lethec (לֶ֫תֶךְ) designates a specific unit of measure in the biblical agrarian world. Its exact origin is not clearly established in Hebrew linguistics. It fits into the system of capacity measures used by the Hebrews, alongside the homer (the largest measure), the ephah (medium measure), and the sack. It is a limited technical term, rarely used in the Bible.
H3963.emploi: The lethec appears only once in the Bible, in Hosea 3:2. In this passage, the prophet Hosea redeems his wife Gomer, who had left him to engage in prostitution. The redemption price includes fifteen shekels of silver as well as a significant quantity of grains: a homer and a lethec of barley. This mention reveals both the economic cost of redemption and the importance of barley as a medium of exchange in the biblical economy. The context of this unique usage is dramatic and rich in symbolic meaning.
H3963.portee: This term illustrates how the Bible is rooted in the concrete reality of the daily and economic life of the people of Israel. It employs the units of measure and material goods that its readers were well acquainted with to tell stories of salvation and love. In Hosea 3, it is through barley and silver that the prophet expresses God's restorative love for His unfaithful people.

sens: What needs to be done, what must be accomplished
An action or thing to be accomplished according to an order or instruction
H3964.detail:
1. What needs to be done, what must be accomplished — The word designates the object of a future action, what constitutes a task or duty. In Ezra 6:8, the Persian king orders the payment of expenses "for what you will have to do": this refers to the action of building the temple, the task imposed on the elders of the Jews.
2. An action or thing to be accomplished according to an order or instruction — The meaning extends to anything that is prescribed, commanded, or necessary: what is appropriate to do in a given situation.
H3964.origine: This Hebrew word belongs to the family of interrogatives and relatives in Hebrew. Originally, it poses the question "what?" or "what is it?", but it can also neutrally designate "that which, what" when it introduces a complement or object. It is a very ancient and common word in the Hebrew Bible.
H3964.emploi: The word appears only once in the Masoretic text with the translation "what" in French. In Ezra 6:8, it is found in a royal decree written in Aramaic (the administrative language of the Persian Empire), where the king gives specific instructions: the payment of construction expenses must be ensured "for what" the elders will have to accomplish. Here, the meaning remains practical and concrete: it is a well-defined administrative and religious task.
H3964.portee: This word reminds us that divine or human orders and instructions always involve a specific task to be accomplished. For the Christian reader, it invites clarity: knowing what one must do is the first step toward obedience. The construction of the temple, financed by the king, shows how God can use even human authorities to fulfill His purposes.

sens: Building or room intended to store grain harvests
Reserve, food depot for the people or the army
Symbol of wealth, abundance, and material security
H3965.detail:
1. A granary is a building or large room where harvests, particularly wheat and grains, are piled and preserved. It is the storage place for the harvests that ensures survival during the coming months (Jeremiah 50:26 speaks of the "granaries" of Babylon as its strategic reserves).
2. By extension, the granary refers to any reserve of food accumulated to feed a people, an army, or an entire nation. These stocks represent the capacity to face famine or to sustain a long period of scarcity.
3. Figuratively, the granary symbolizes prosperity, abundance, and security — which is why its destruction (like that of Babylon) signifies complete ruin and the inability to survive.
H3965.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes accumulation, storage. It concretely designates the place where harvests are gathered and preserved, a central image in an agricultural culture where wealth is measured by the size of the harvests and the ability to preserve them.
H3965.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 50:26, where the prophet describes the future destruction of Babylon: God commands to enter its granaries, to turn them into heaps of rubble like sheaves of wheat. The image is violent: the reserves of a world power, symbolizing its wealth and solidity, will be reduced to nothing. This passage situates the granary at the heart of a nation's economic and military life.
H3965.portee: This word reminds us that true security does not lie in the accumulation of material goods. The destruction of Babylon's granaries illustrates the biblical teaching: no human reserve, however impressive, can withstand God's judgment. For the Christian, this invites not to place hope in wealth, but in divine providence.

sens: In large quantity, abundantly
To a high degree, much
In an intense or powerful manner
With force, firmly
H3966.detail:
1. The word describes what exists in large quantity or abundance. In Genesis 13:2, Abraham was "very" rich in livestock and silver; in Exodus 12:38, a "great" multitude went up with the Israelites. The idea is one of accumulation, of profusion.
2. It indicates a high degree or marked intensity: something that exceeds the ordinary measure. In Genesis 1:31, God saw that everything was "very" good; in Exodus 14:10, the children of Israel were "greatly" afraid. It is a degree that strikes, that moves.
3. It serves to reinforce the idea of power or impact: what is done with force or has a powerful effect. In Exodus 9:24, the hail was "very" violent; in Joshua 10:2, Gibeon was a "very" great city. This touches on vigor, intensity.
4. Placed before an imperative or a verb, it expresses a firm exhortation, a pressing obligation. In Deuteronomy 6:5, it is about loving the Lord "with all" your heart; in Psalms 119:4, observing the ordinances "carefully". It is a call to total commitment.
H3966.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root meaning first "strength" or "power". Its original meaning is that of vigor, of what weighs heavily, of what imposes itself. From there, it has evolved to express any notion of greatness, of high degree, of quantity that exceeds the normal. The word belongs to an ancient Semitic family that linked the idea of physical strength with that of intensity or metaphorical weight.
H3966.emploi: This word is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible, appearing about 278 times. It appears in all types of texts: historical narratives, laws, poetry, prophecy. Often it reinforces an adjective ("very good", "very fat") or a noun ("great fear", "great multitude"). Sometimes it is used alone as an adverb ("exceedingly"). In the laws of Deuteronomy, it marks the intensity of an obligation or a warning: keep your heart "carefully" (Deuteronomy 4:9). In poetry, it emphasizes the scope of an emotion or a divine action.
H3966.portee: This word reminds us that God perceives the world in terms of intense quality. When He saw that everything was "very" good on the sixth day, this judgment expresses complete satisfaction that speaks to our hearts. To love the Lord "with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength" is not a lukewarm request: it is a call to total commitment, to the power of the heart. This word invites us to live with intensity, without stinginess or lukewarmness.

sens: Whole number equal to ten times ten
Used in composition to form other numbers (two hundred, three hundred, etc.)
Fraction of a unit (one hundredth)
Considerable size, multitude or abundance in a figurative sense
H3967.detail:
1. The number hundred is simply the digit 100, the basic numerical unit for counting large groups: Adam was a hundred thirty years old when he fathered Seth (Genesis 5:3).
2. Hundred is part of the composition of larger numbers: Solomon had fourteen hundred chariots (1 Kings 10:26), or Abijah engaged in battle with four hundred thousand men (2 Chronicles 13:3).
3. The word can also refer to a part divided into a hundred (one hundredth), although this usage is rare in the provided texts.
4. Beyond simple counting, hundred symbolizes a multitude or an overwhelming force: when five of you chase a hundred, and a hundred thousand chase ten thousand, it is the image of supernatural power (Leviticus 26:8).
H3967.origine: The Hebrew word מֵאָה (méah) comes from a root meaning "to fill" or "to be full." This origin reflects the idea that a hundred is a "fullness" or a complete unit capable of filling space. The word also appears in Aramaic (מְאָה, méah) with the same meaning. It is a fundamental number in the Hebrew numerical system, used since the earliest genealogies in the Bible.
H3967.emploi: The word hundred appears over 500 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in genealogical accounts (Genesis 5, 11) where it expresses the ages of the patriarchs before and after the Flood. It is ubiquitous in military (Exodus 12:37, 2 Chronicles 13:3) and administrative counts (Exodus 18:21), forming the basis of numbers in hundreds of soldiers or leaders. Its meaning remains always numerical and positive, serving to quantify lifespans, goods, troops, or constructions (dimensions of the tabernacle, Exodus 27). Rarely, it can indicate a tiny proportion (one hundredth) or simply express the notion of a great multitude.
H3967.portee: For the Christian reader, the number hundred in the genealogy of the patriarchs reminds us that God granted extraordinarily long lives to the ancient faithful, testifying to His providence before the Flood. In the promises of military blessing (Leviticus 26:8), this number illustrates how divine strength multiplies the effectiveness of believers and overturns numerical inequality by the power of God. It is a lesson in trust: depending on the Lord produces disproportionate strength.

sens: Fortified tower of the northern wall of Jerusalem
Landmark of the wall reconstructed by Nehemiah
H3968.detail:
1. Meah (which means "Hundred") is a defensive tower built on the northern part of the wall of Jerusalem, on the rampart that Nehemiah had rebuilt upon returning from exile. It served to monitor and protect this section of the wall.
2. The tower of Meah appears as an important geographical landmark during the reconstruction of the gates of Jerusalem: it marks a boundary between different sections of the work site (Nehemiah 3:1) and is mentioned again during the dedication procession of the wall (Nehemiah 12:39), showing its importance in the city's topography.
H3968.origine: The Hebrew word "meah" simply means "hundred." The tower likely received this name either because it was the hundredth from a reference point, or because its height was a hundred cubits, or due to another numerical characteristic. The name reflects the simple way the Ancients designated places by numbers or distinctive traits.
H3968.emploi: Meah appears only twice in the Bible, both in the book of Nehemiah, directly related to the restoration of the wall of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. In Nehemiah 3:1, it marks the starting point (or a boundary) of the northern section of the wall that the priests rebuilt, from the Sheep Gate to the tower of Hananel. In Nehemiah 12:39, it is mentioned again during the dedication procession of the restored wall, confirming its role as a geographical landmark and key fortification of the city.

sens: Whole number equal to ten times ten
A very large quantity, a multitude
H3969.detail:
1. "Hundred" is the number 100, formed from ten groups of ten. This number appears in precise enumerations, notably in the counts of offerings for the temple: in Ezra 6:17, "one hundred bulls" are offered for the dedication of the temple of God, alongside two hundred rams and four hundred lambs — the detail of the numbers shows that it is an exact and solemn counting.
2. The word can also evoke a large quantity, almost immeasurable, when used to speak of a multitude. In Daniel 6:1, the king establishes "one hundred twenty satraps" to govern the kingdom — this is a high number that underscores the extent of the administration.
H3969.origine: This Aramaic word (méah) is closely related to its Hebrew equivalent מֵאָה (meah), which also means "hundred." It is a simple word, without a complex root: it directly designates the number, like other digits. It is found in both Semitic languages of the biblical text with the same meaning and pronunciation.
H3969.emploi: The word appears three times in the Aramaic portions of the Bible (Ezra and Daniel). In Ezra 6:17 and 7:22, it is used to count offerings at the temple and resources that the king provides: these are contexts of administrative and cultic precision. In Daniel 6:1, it counts the high officials of the kingdom. Each time, "hundred" or its multiples ("one hundred twenty") mark a determined quantity, never approximate — it is the language of those who keep accounts.
H3969.portee: The number "hundred" reminds us that the Bible pays attention to concrete and measurable things: resources, offerings, organization. For the believer, this underscores that our service to God is also expressed in the concrete and the detail, like these animals offered with care, or like the order that God brings to human affairs through His servants.

sens: Intense wish, ardent longing
What one wishes to obtain or accomplish
Covetousness, evil desire directed against others
H3970.detail:
1. Desire is an intense wish, a longing that arises from deep within the heart — a movement of the will towards something that attracts us. It is the impulse of the heart that aims at a goal: to possess, to enjoy, to accomplish.
2. Desire also concretely designates what one wishes: the very thing one covets, what one burns to obtain or to do. In Psalms 140:9, the wicked harbors desires against his enemies — malicious plans he is eager to carry out.
3. Desire often takes on a negative coloring: it is covetousness, the will to do evil that drives one to wish harm to others or to violate justice. This meaning strongly emerges in Psalms 140:9, where the psalmist asks God not to let the wicked's criminal desires come to fruition.
H3970.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing fervor, the impulse of desire. It is related to other Hebrew words denoting inclinations or wills of the heart. It is a common term in the Bible to express the interiority of the being — what moves, drives, attracts, or repels it.
H3970.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 140:9. In this context, it qualifies the wicked's evil intentions — his hostile plans against those who oppose him. The psalmist, in danger, pleads with the Lord to thwart these malevolent desires and prevent the criminal from triumphing. The word emphasizes that evil proceeds from a deliberate will, from a covetousness of the heart, and not from a mere passing error.
H3970.portee: This word reminds us that human will is at the heart of our actions — desire reveals what truly animates us. The text invites the believer to examine their own desires: do we seek good or evil? Are our intentions directed towards God and justice, or towards envy and malice? It is an encouragement to pray to God to transform our desires and to keep us from devastating covetousness.

sens: Physical stain or impurity that tarnishes
Visible defect, bodily infirmity
Moral imperfection, guilt of the heart
H3971A.detail:
1. A stain or impurity that attaches to something — like a mark that soils it: in Job 31:7, Job asserts that no stain has attached to his hands, meaning he has not committed any dishonest or impure act.
2. A visible defect of the body, an infirmity or scar that renders it imperfect: Daniel 1:4 speaks of young boys without physical defect, meaning physically intact and beautiful, worthy to serve the king.
3. A moral imperfection or guilt that stains the soul — the image of the stain extends from the body to the conscience: when Job protests his innocence, he rejects any stain in the sense of a bad act.
H3971A.origine: The Hebrew word m.um primarily denotes a visible stain, a mark that disfigures. It comes from a root that evokes the idea of something damaged or degraded. In biblical language, the stain can be literal (a wound, a scar) or moral (a sin, a transgression): Scripture often speaks of the heart stained by evil, as if sin leaves an invisible yet real mark.
H3971A.emploi: This word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible: in Job 31:7, where Job asks God to examine his hands and eyes and swears that no stain has attached to them (image of the body stained by dishonest acts), and in Daniel 1:4, where he describes the candidates for the king's service as young men without physical defect (image of the intact and healthy body). The meaning thus shifts between a visible physical imperfection and a moral impurity: one diverts a body from its natural perfection, the other diverts a soul from good.
H3971A.portee: This word shows us that the Bible considers the whole person — body and soul — as capable of being stained or purified. For the believer, it reminds us that sin is not an abstraction, but something that marks and wounds; and that God's grace, like water that washes a stain, can cleanse this impurity if we repent.

sens: Physical imperfection of the body
Injury or wound inflicted on someone
Moral stain or impurity
H3971B.detail:
1. Physical defect is a malformation, an infirmity, or a mutilation of the body that renders it imperfect: lameness, blindness, or any visible deformity. The law commands that a priest with such a defect cannot approach the altar to offer sacrifices (Leviticus 21:17), and that no sacrifice offered should have a defect (Leviticus 22:20).
2. An injury or wound is a defect caused by a blow or violence: the law of retaliation — eye for eye, tooth for tooth — commands to inflict the same injury that was inflicted (Leviticus 24:20).
3. Moral defect is a stain or spiritual blemish in character: the generation of Israel is described as perverse and impure, "a crooked and depraved generation" (Deuteronomy 32:5).
H3971B.origine: The Hebrew word מוּם (mum) literally denotes a visible defect, a mark or notch that spoils the perfection of something or someone.
