It comes from a root evoking the idea of damage or destruction. This word is used in the sacrificial laws of the Old Testament to express the divine requirement of purity and perfection in worship.
H3971B.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the Old Testament, concentrated mainly in the books of the law (Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Numbers). It is first used in a physical and concrete sense: the law requires that priests and sacrificial victims be free from any visible defect, as the defect renders one unworthy to approach God or unacceptable for worship (Leviticus 21-22, Deuteronomy 15:21). Once, it designates the injury inflicted by vengeance (Leviticus 24:20). In a few passages, it takes on a moral or spiritual sense: Deuteronomy 32:5 speaks of a generation that bears the defect of betrayal against God, and Song of Solomon 4:7 celebrates the absence of defect in the beloved.
H3971B.portee: This word reminds us of the biblical requirement for holiness: access to God demands purity, both in the acts of worship and in the heart. It confronts us with our own imperfection and our need for grace. It also announces that only what is perfect is worthy of God, an expectation that the Incarnation of Christ — without blemish or defect — will fully accomplish.

sens: total absence of something
absence of action or intention
nothingness, nonexistence
loss of value, insignificance
H3972.detail:
1. The word expresses complete absence: nothing exists, nothing is present. When the angel says to Abraham "do nothing to him," it means: do no harm to the child, not even the slightest gesture (Genesis 22:12).
2. It can also denote the absence of action or intention: Joseph asserts that he has done "nothing" to deserve prison, meaning he has committed no fault (Genesis 40:15). Samuel protests that nothing has been found in his hands, in other words, that he has stolen from no one (1 Samuel 12:5).
3. The word sometimes emphasizes the slightest attempt, the shadow of an action: Amnon cannot make "the slightest attempt" against Tamar because she is a virgin (2 Samuel 13:2). It is the nothingness of possible action.
4. It also expresses insignificance: in Solomon's time, money had "no value," meaning no worth, because gold was so abundant (2 Chronicles 9:20).
H3972.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "nothing" or "void." It is related to other Hebrew terms for absence or nonexistence. The word carries the primary idea of what is not, which counts for nothing. It is a very classic term to express nothingness in biblical language.
H3972.emploi: The word appears 32 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the narratives of Genesis, Samuel, and in contexts where it is about denying an action, a possession, or a guilt. It is also found in wisdom literature like Ecclesiastes, which meditates on the nothingness of human things. Its meaning is very stable: it always means "nothing" or "none." It can refer to an action (doing nothing), a possession (owning nothing), a discovery (finding nothing), or a value (counting for nothing). The Segond translates this word as "nothing," "none," or "least" depending on the context.
H3972.portee: This simple yet powerful word reminds us that the absence of guilt or evil is a precious good: that is why Joseph and Samuel protest that they have done "nothing" wrong. It also invites us to consider the insignificance of riches before God — the countless gold of Solomon was ultimately just nothing. Finally, it expresses the force of divine negation: when God says "do nothing," it is an absolute command that requires total obedience.

sens: Feeling of aversion or rejection towards someone or something
Contempt or public humiliation
H3973.detail:
1. Disdain is that feeling of rejection and aversion one experiences towards what is considered unworthy, repugnant, or worthless. It is to look at something or someone from a height, with a mixture of contempt and disgust. In Lamentations 3:45, the people of Israel, after the destruction of Jerusalem, complain of being treated as an object of disdain among the nations — rejected, despised, unworthy of consideration.
2. Disdain also refers to public humiliation, the act of being treated as something worthless, contemptible. It is the concrete experience of being despised and rejected by others, a humiliation that socially marks one.
H3973.origine: The Hebrew word maos comes from a root that means "to reject" or "to push away." This family of words evokes the idea of turning one's back on something, pushing it away as unacceptable. The word carries with it the image of physical rejection, then moral and emotional rejection. It is related to Hebrew verbs that express refusal or aversion.
H3973.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible in Hebrew, in the context of lamentations over the fall of Jerusalem. The suffering people cry out their experience of humiliation: they have been reduced to an object of disdain in the eyes of neighboring nations. This context of extreme suffering shows how disdain is perceived as a form of spiritual and social degradation, a dehumanization. The disdain of others becomes a major wound for the one who endures it.
H3973.portee: This word invites the reader to measure the depth of Israel's suffering and, more broadly, that of any humiliated people. It also reminds us that the contempt of others deeply wounds. For the Christian, it highlights the empathy that God has for the humiliated: Jesus himself experienced disdain and humiliation (Matthew 27:29-31), transforming this experience into redemption.

sens: Celestial body that emits light
Object that produces light through a flame
One who shines, illuminates, or guides
H3974.detail:
1. A luminary primarily refers to a celestial body: the sun and the moon that God placed in the sky to illuminate the earth and mark the passage of time (Genesis 1:14-16). The image is that of a heavenly source shining upon all creation.
2. The word also applies to the lampstand of the sanctuary, the gold furniture equipped with lamps that were lit to illuminate the inside of the tent of meeting (Exodus 27:20). Each lamp was a small luminary casting its light in the holy place.
3. More broadly, a luminary is that which shines and illuminates, which lights up the darkness and guides the way. This is why the term can refer to one who brings light, in a figurative sense: a person who shows the way or clarifies the heart (Proverbs 15:30).
H3974.origine: The word comes from the root אור (or), which means "to shine" or "to give light." It expresses the simple action of lighting, of what becomes visible thanks to a light source. The Hebrew term מָאוֹר (maor) literally means "that which produces light" or "that which shines." It is an agent noun formed to show the effect of this light: that which glows, that which illuminates.
H3974.emploi: The word maor appears 16 times in the Bible, primarily for three usages. First, at the origins of the world: God creates the celestial luminaries (the sun and the moon) to illuminate and regulate time (Genesis 1:14-16). Next, in the law of the sanctuary: it refers to the lampstand of the tabernacle, fueled with olive oil, whose lamps burned continually before the Lord (Exodus 25:6; 27:20; 35:14). Finally, in poetic imagery: the luminary becomes a symbol of strength or glory (Ezekiel 32:8) or of what makes good and evil visible (Psalms 90:8). The meaning remains concrete but is enriched with religious and symbolic nuances.
H3974.portee: This word reminds the believer that God creates light and that all that shines comes from His hand. The lampstand of the sanctuary, as a perpetual luminary, symbolizes the presence and divine illumination at the heart of the people. The luminary invites reflection on spiritual light: that which guides, exposes hidden truth, and allows one to see the way. It is a call to be a luminary for others, to reflect divine light.

sens: Hole, cavity, refuge of an animal
Lair of a serpent or beast
Figuratively: hidden dwelling, asylum
H3975.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a hole or natural cave, a refuge where an animal retreats. It is a place dug into the earth or rock, dark and sheltered.
2. The Bible particularly uses it for the lair of serpents or wild beasts — dangerous creatures that hide in their dens. In Isaiah 11:8, it refers to the den of the basilisk, that legendary feared serpent.
3. The image can become figurative to designate any dwelling, an asylum where one withdraws, especially a dark and unsettling place.
H3975.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes darkness and cavity. The basic meaning is "hole" or "opening" — the idea of a hollow and closed space. The form here (with the prefix m-) is constructed to designate the result or place: hence "hole," "den." The Greek translates this word with terms meaning "hole" or "cave."
H3975.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 11:8. The prophet paints a vision of messianic peace where little children play fearlessly near the most dangerous creatures — vipers and basilisks — without running any peril. The "den" or "cave" of the serpent then becomes a place of harmless play. It is a context of radical transformation of the world, where even the lair of evil beasts loses its threat.
H3975.portee: This verse shows that the redemption brought by the Messiah transforms even the natural order: dangerous creatures lose their power to harm. For the reader, this reveals the extent of the promised restoration — it concerns not only humans but all of creation. It is a promise of absolute peace and security in the coming kingdom.

sens: Instrument à deux plateaux pour peser
Mesure, poids
Équilibre, impartialité
Insignifiance relative
H3976.detail:
1. The balance is the practical instrument of commerce and daily life: two plates suspended from a beam or scale, where goods are placed on one side and reference weights on the other until equilibrium is reached (Leviticus 19:36: "You shall have just balances, just weights"). It is the tool that the barber or cook used to weigh precisely.
2. By extension, "balance" refers to the act of weighing, the determination of weight or value (Ezekiel 5:1: "Take a balance for weighing, and divide the hair").
3. Figuratively, the balance represents equity and righteousness: a just balance is a symbol of integral justice, while a false balance (using different weights depending on the direction of the exchange) expresses dishonesty (Proverbs 11:1: "A false balance is an abomination to the Lord, but a just weight is his delight").
4. The image of the balance also evokes the insignificance of certain things in light of reality: the nations before God are light as dust on a balance, meaning negligible in weight and importance (Isaiah 40:15: "The nations are like a drop from a bucket... like dust on the scales").
H3976.origine: The Hebrew word moazen (מֹאזֵן) comes from the root azoun (עזן), which means "to weigh." The Aramaic uses the same family with mouzonaya (מֹאזְנַיָּא). Like many Hebrew tools, the word first designates the concrete object, then becomes an image of judgment, balance, and justice — the balance being the instrument by which one "judges" the weight of things.
H3976.emploi: The word appears 15 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the laws of Leviticus (just weights), the wisdom of Proverbs (moral correctness), and the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Amos, Micah, Hosea). In legal or commercial contexts, the just balance is required by the Law of Moses as an expression of righteousness towards one's neighbor (Leviticus 19:36, Ezekiel 45:10). In wisdom literature, the false balance embodies lies, fraud, and injustice (Proverbs 11:1, 16:11, 20:23). In prophetic contexts, Isaiah and Ezekiel use the image to evoke divine measurement or the relative insignificance of the earthly world. Job invokes God's balance to demand that his integrity be weighed justly (Job 31:6).
H3976.portee: The balance teaches the believer that God sees and judges with perfect accuracy: nothing escapes his "balance." Concretely, this word reminds us that righteousness involves practical honesty in exchanges, the absence of double standards, and equity towards the poor and weak. It invites reflection on what has weight before God: justice, faithfulness, and integrity are worth infinitely more than wealth or appearance.

sens: Sharp instrument with a fixed blade, equipped with a handle, used for cutting
Weapon or instrument of death
Metaphorically, that which wounds or devours
H3979.detail:
1. A knife is primarily a practical tool for cutting: Abraham carries one during the sacrifice of Isaac, holding it in his hand alongside the fire and the wood (Genesis 22:6). It is a common object in the ancient world.
2. The same object becomes a weapon of death when Abraham "took the knife to slay his son" (Genesis 22:10). In a dramatic context, this sharp tool embodies violence: a man takes a knife to dismember his concubine (Judges 19:29), an act of extreme brutality.
3. The Bible also uses "knife" in a figurative sense: the teeth of a certain race are compared to "swords" and their jaws to "knives," a poetic image to express their cruelty towards the poor (Proverbs 30:14). The knife symbolizes here that which devours and wounds.
H3979.origine: The Hebrew word מַאֲכֶלֶת (maakélet) comes from the root אכל (akhal), which means "to eat" or "to devour." A knife is therefore literally "that which is used to eat," the instrument that divides meat. This root also appears in maakhal (food). The basic image is that of the tool that allows for the preparation and consumption of food.
H3979.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible, always translated as "knife" by the Segond translators. Genesis 22 uses it for the foundational episode of the sacrifice of Isaac: the knife is the instrument of the ultimate test imposed by God on Abraham. Judges 19 employs it in a context of extreme violence, an act of bloody vengeance. Proverbs 30 takes the word out of its literal usage to make a poetic image of devouring. The word always designates a concrete sharp object, never a sword or a weapon of war.
H3979.portee: The sacrifice of Isaac in Genesis 22 makes the knife a symbol of absolute sacrifice: it is with this simple tool that Abraham's faith in God is engaged. For the Christian reader, this knife recalls the cost of renunciation and obedience. The contrast between Genesis 22 (where the knife is not used) and Judges 19 also shows how the same object can serve good or evil depending on the heart of the one who uses it.

sens: That which fire devours, what feeds it
Material consumed by flames
Figuratively, that which is destined to be destroyed
H3980.detail:
1. This word literally designates what fire eats, what nourishes it and keeps it burning. In Isaiah 9:4, the blood-soaked war garments are described as being delivered to the flames to be "devoured" by fire: it is as if the fire is hungry for these garments and consumes them.
2. The word more broadly evokes anything that is consumed by flames, anything that burns. It is the combustible material that fire transforms into ash.
3. Figuratively and prophetically, it refers to what is condemned to destruction. In Isaiah 9:18, the people are described as the "prey" of divine fire: the fire of the Lord's anger treats them as its food, its game to devour.
H3980.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to eat" or "to devour" (used for food, but also for fire that "eats" what it consumes). It is a word from the family of terms that evoke food and feasting. The prefix gives the word the sense of food intended for someone or something — in this case, for fire.
H3980.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, both in Isaiah 9, in a passage that describes the destructions of war and divine anger. The first occurrence (verse 4) speaks concretely of military garments burned by fire. The second (verse 18) transposes the image: fire becomes the agent of divine judgment, and the people become its prey. It is a vocabulary of judgment and total destruction.
H3980.portee: This image of fire that devours reminds us that the destruction of evil is complete and definitive. For the biblical reader, it also shows the gravity of divine anger — it leaves nothing remaining of what it consumes. It is an invitation to fear the Lord and not to despise His judgment.

sens: Physical power or capacity for action
Energy, vigor
Figuratively: power, influence
H3981.detail:
1. This word designates physical strength or the concrete ability to act and produce an effect: it is the power that can be deployed. In Job 36:19, Eliphaz asks Job if even "all the strength you could muster" would be enough to deliver him from his distress — he speaks of the energy and vigor that Job could mobilize.
2. The word can also evoke effort, the power exerted to accomplish something: it is less the state of strength than the energetic action of strength.
3. Figuratively, it designates power or influence, the capacity to impose one's will or produce a lasting effect.
H3981.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of firmness and solidity. It is constructed with a prefix that intensifies its meaning. The concept of strength in the Bible always evokes a real and concrete capacity, not abstract: it is a power that can be seen at work.
H3981.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 36:19, in the discourse of the character Eliphaz. In this context of suffering and illness, it serves to show that human strength — no matter how great — cannot always deliver us from our distresses. It is a rare word that underscores the impotence of our own strength in the face of the deepest realities.
H3981.portee: This verse teaches us that our personal strength, even when fully deployed, is not always the answer to our greatest difficulties. Only the wisdom and power of God can deliver us from them — a valuable lesson for the Christian who tends to rely first on their own resources.

sens: That which is commanded, prescribed by someone in authority
An instruction, a directive to follow
A command, a public or official edict
H3982.detail:
1. That which is commanded, prescribed by someone in authority — The word designates what a person invested with power imposes on another. In Esther 1:15, King Ahasuerus gives an "order" to Queen Vashti through the eunuchs: it is his royal command, his imperative instruction.
2. An instruction, a directive to follow — The word can also designate a guideline or a prohibition that is transmitted to someone trustworthy. In Esther 2:20, Mordecai had given "orders" to Esther (particularly not to reveal her origins), and she observed them scrupulously, as a young girl obeys her guardian.
3. A command, a public or official edict — The word also applies to a decree or solemn decision that is promulgated. In Esther 9:32, Esther's "order" regarding the Feast of Purim is recorded in the official archives of the kingdom, confirming its institution.
H3982.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to say" or "to speak" (אמר), from which emerges the idea of what is stated, declared, and thus imposed as instruction. Aramaic uses a similar form (מֵאמַר, me.mar) with the same meaning of a word that becomes a command. It is a typical word of official and administrative texts.
H3982.emploi: The word appears three times in the Bible, only in the book of Esther, which tells the story of the Jewish queen at the court of Persian King Ahasuerus. It is used in contexts of authority: that of the king over his subjects, that of Mordecai over his ward Esther, and that of Esther herself when she becomes queen and transmits her own decrees. It is an administrative and official word, characteristic of the Persian context of the book.
H3982.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of obedience to authority, whether royal, familial, or communal. In particular, Esther's faithfulness to Mordecai's "orders" shows that humble and constant obedience can serve God's purposes in the background. It is also an example of how an authorized word becomes law and transforms reality.

sens: Commandment or directive given by an authority
Thing provided or delivered according to a request
Decision made by a heavenly or divine power
H3983.detail:
1. The word designates an order or command issued by someone who has authority. It is a directive that others must follow. In Daniel 4:17, the "sentence" and the "resolution" of the heavenly beings who watch are divine orders that govern what happens on earth.
2. It can also mean what is provided or delivered in response to a request. In Ezra 6:9, the necessary provisions for sacrifices — bulls, rams, lambs, wheat, salt, wine, and oil — are to be "delivered" to the priests each day according to their needs.
3. More broadly, it is a resolution or sentence: a decision made by an authority that must be fulfilled. The order of heaven is executed unfailingly on earth.
H3983.origine: This Aramaic word comes from an older Hebrew root (maamar, H3982) which literally means "word" or "thing said." The basic image is that of a word that comes from the mouth of an authority and becomes a command that others obey. In both Hebrew and Aramaic, it is a term that connects the word to power: to say is to command when one has authority.
H3983.emploi: This word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the books of the post-exilic period written in Aramaic. In Ezra 6:9, it refers to the delivery of provisions for the Temple worship — it is an administrative order that must be executed regularly. In Daniel 4:17, it takes on a mystical and cosmic dimension: it is the order of the heavenly beings, a divine resolution that determines the course of human kingdoms. The word thus plays on two registers: practical order and cosmic order.
H3983.portee: This word reminds the believer that God speaks and that His word is fulfilled. The orders of the Most High, invisible to the eyes of men, govern empires and events. Recognizing the divine order means accepting that God reigns far beyond what we see.

sens: Object shaped to serve a specific purpose
Container intended to hold or pour
Object of worship or service in the temple
H3984.detail:
1. The word designates any object made and intended to fulfill a specific function: it is a generic term for talking about a tool or equipment. In Ezra 7:19, Ezra must "deposit before the God of Jerusalem the utensils that are entrusted to you for the service of the house of your God": these are concrete objects, intended for use.
2. More specifically, it is a vessel or container — generally made of precious metal — designed to hold or pour liquid. When Belshazzar "had the gold and silver vessels brought" from the temple of Jerusalem in Daniel 5:2, these are cups, pitchers, or dishes for libations and meals.
3. In the context of the temple, these utensils are not mere household objects, but sacred furnishings, consecrated to the worship of God. Their deportation to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar (Ezra 5:14) and their subsequent restitution (Ezra 6:5) mark the religious importance of these objects in the life of the Jewish community.
H3984.origine: The Hebrew word מָאן comes from a root that means "to prepare" or "to arrange": it is something that has been prepared, shaped for a purpose. It belongs to the family of terms designating shaped objects, as opposed to natural things. In Greek, the translators of the Septuagint often used ἀγγεῖον (vessel) or σκεῦος (utensil, equipment) to render this word.
H3984.emploi: This word appears 7 times in biblical Hebrew, almost exclusively in the accounts of the deportation and restoration of the temple in Jerusalem (Ezra and Daniel). It concretely designates the vessels and containers of the temple — objects of gold and silver — that Nebuchadnezzar took away during the destruction of Jerusalem. The word regularly returns when the text speaks of their restitution under the reign of Cyrus (Ezra 5:14-15; 6:5) or their desecration during Belshazzar's feast (Daniel 5:2-3). The repeated use of the same term emphasizes the symbolic and historical importance of these objects for the restoration of worship.
H3984.portee: These utensils remind the Christian reader that the legitimate worship of God needs its own place and tools: God is not indifferent to the means we use to honor Him. The deportation of these vessels also illustrates how human powers may seem to triumph momentarily, but God restores what belongs to Him. Finally, the desecration of the vessels in Daniel 5 shows that treating with contempt the things consecrated to God has consequences.

sens: to say no to someone, not to accept what is proposed or offered
not wanting to do what is asked, opposing it
to push away, reject a person or a thing
to obstinately resist something, to stand firm against it
H3985.detail:
1. The verb refuse primarily designates the act of saying no, of pushing away an offer or proposal. Naaman urges Elisha to accept a gift, "but he refused" (2 Kings 5:16): he simply rejects what is presented to him. Jacob, inconsolable after the loss of Joseph, "would not receive any consolation" (Genesis 37:35): he refuses even the efforts of his family to comfort him.
2. The word also expresses a refusal to obey, a refusal to do what is asked. The Lord asks Pharaoh: "How long will you refuse to observe my commandments and my laws?" (Exodus 16:28). The people of Israel "refused to listen to the voice of Samuel" (1 Samuel 8:19): they do not want to listen, they refuse to do so.
3. It can also mean to reject, to push away in a stronger sense: to refuse not only a proposal but a person themselves, or to send them far away. It is a form of rejection or distancing.
4. Finally, refuse expresses a tenacious resistance, an obstinacy. Wisdom says: "I call and you resist" (Proverbs 1:24) — you refuse to listen to me despite my repeated calls. It is a hardening, a persistent closing off.
H3985.origine: The Hebrew verb māên (ם-א-נ) belongs to a family of words expressing the idea of refusal, of saying no, of opposing. The root suggests a firm will, an act of the will that pushes away. In Piel (the active intensive form of the verb), it reinforces the idea: not only does one refuse passively, but one actively refuses, one pushes away. It is the decided rejection, the affirmed opposition. The word appears 39 times in the Old Testament and remains constant in its meaning: always this notion of rejection, of non-acceptance.
H3985.emploi: The verb refuse appears 39 times in the Old Testament, especially in the historical books (Samuel, Kings), the prophets (especially Jeremiah, Isaiah, Hosea), and the wisdom literature (Proverbs, Psalms). The usages are distributed in three main contexts: the refusal of people towards others (accepting a gift, a consolation, advice), the refusal of obedience towards God or His commandments, and the refusal of conversion despite prophetic calls. In Jeremiah notably, the people "refuse to convert" (8:5), they "refuse instruction" (5:3), just as Hosea shows that Israel "refuses to return" (11:5). It is therefore a word of hardening and disobedience: it paints the attitude of one who closes their heart to God or to their neighbor.
H3985.portee: This word confronts us with the seriousness of refusal: to refuse is never neutral. When Israel refuses to listen to God and His prophets, this repeated refusal creates a hardening of the heart, an obstinacy that leads to ruin. But it also reminds us of our responsibility: at every call from God, we have the power to say yes or no. The refusal of God is the essence of disobedience; conversely, our consent to listen and obey is the path to blessing.

sens: To not consent to do something, to oppose it
To reject a request, an order
To show disobedience or rebellion
H3986.detail:
1. To refuse is to say no to someone who asks or commands. It expresses a clear refusal, a definite opposition. This is what Pharaoh does when Moses asks him to let the people of Israel go: "If you refuse to let them go, I will strike you with frogs" (Exodus 7:27). The word describes the act of saying no in the face of authority, in this case, that of God speaking through Moses.
2. To refuse can also mean to push away something that is offered or imposed upon us. This goes beyond a simple "no": it is an act of will to set aside or reject. When one refuses to go out, as Jeremiah tells Zedekiah, one is deliberately choosing not to obey (Jeremiah 38:21).
3. Refusal often expresses rebellion or disobedience. Pharaoh refuses not out of hesitation, but out of a hardened heart: he refuses three times in a row (Exodus 7:27; 9:2; 10:4), showing fierce opposition to the divine will.
H3986.origine: The Hebrew verb מָאֵן (maën) comes from a root that expresses rejection and opposition. In the Hebrew Bible, this word is used to describe a conscious and active refusal, never a simple inability or external obstacle. It is related to other Hebrew terms for refusal but is distinguished by its tone of insubordination or hardening.
H3986.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the Bible, all concentrated in two parallel passages of the plague narrative (Exodus 7-10) and a prophetic word (Jeremiah 38). Three times, it is Pharaoh who refuses to let Israel go, showing how his refusal worsens as God sends successive plagues. This repeated refusal becomes a central motif: the more the plagues strike, the more Pharaoh hardens and refuses. The last occurrence, in Jeremiah, transposes this meaning to Zedekiah, the king of Judah, who refuses to submit to Jeremiah's words. In all cases, refusal is presented as disobedience to God's commands or words.
H3986.portee: This word reminds us that refusing the word of God leads to consequences. Pharaoh's refusal did not stop the plagues; on the contrary, it brought judgment upon judgment. For the Christian reader, it serves as a warning: yielding to disobedience, rejecting God's commands, is to harden oneself and expose oneself to judgment. But it is also an invitation not to refuse: obeying what God asks is to avoid this path of rebellion.

sens: To not want to do something, to reject a request or an order
To disdainfully reject someone or something
To deliberately oppose the will of God
H3987.detail:
1. To refuse is to say no, to not want to obey a request or an order. The word describes an act of will: one could do it, but chooses not to. In Jeremiah 13:10, the wicked people "refuse to listen" to the words of God — they hear them, but they voluntarily reject them.
2. Refusal can pertain to a person: one pushes them away, one disdains them. It is an act of hostility or disdain.
3. In the Bible, to refuse often has a spiritual significance: it is to oppose God Himself, to turn away from His commandments and choose one's own path.
H3987.origine: The Hebrew word מֵאֵן (mé'ène) comes from the root אנן, which expresses the idea of saying no, of turning away. Its primary meaning is purely voluntary: it is not incapacity, but choice. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this verb often describes the refusal to obey God or to listen to Him.
H3987.emploi: This word appears only once in the Greek New Testament (in the form of Jeremiah 13:10), but it is common in the Hebrew Old Testament to describe the refusal to listen to God. In Jeremiah 13:10, the people of Israel deliberately refuse the words of the Lord: they could obey, but they choose to follow "the inclinations of their heart" and worship other gods. The context shows that this is a culpable refusal, provoking divine anger.
H3987.portee: This word reminds the reader that sin begins with a choice: man is not forced to disobey God; he refuses to listen to Him. It is a refusal of the divine will that holds accountable the one who rejects the word of the Lord. For the Christian, this invites examination of one's own refusals — where one says no to God instead of yes.

sens: To refuse or push away something that is offered or proposed to us
To disdain someone or something, treating it as worthless or unworthy
To abandon someone, to forsake them, to cease supporting or cherishing them
To deliberately violate or transgress a covenant, a commitment
H3988A.detail:
1. To refuse or actively push something away: it is to say no, to not want to accept. Thus, in 1 Samuel 8:7, the Lord tells Samuel that the people have "rejected" Him, refusing to acknowledge Him as king.
2. To disdain is to regard something or someone as despicable, worthless, or unworthy of consideration. Job's servant asks in Job 31:13 if he has ever "despised" the rights of his servants during a dispute — treating them as if they did not deserve to be heard.
3. To abandon or forsake someone is to cease supporting, loving, or caring for them. Isaiah 54:6 speaks of a "rejected" woman — the Lord calls her back because she has been abandoned. This is an emotional and relational rejection.
4. To deliberately transgress a covenant or divine command is to "despise" them willingly. In Leviticus 26:15, to despise the laws and ordinances of the Lord is to refuse to keep them, breaking the commitment made before God.
H3988A.origine: The Hebrew verb מָאַס (maas) describes the movement of pushing something away, holding it at a distance, saying no. Its root evokes the idea of turning away, refusing to accept. In Hebrew, the word is used for both passive rejection (being rejected) and active rejection (to reject). When the Lord "rejects" Israel, it is a voluntary act of rupture; when Israel "rejects" the word of the Lord, it is an act of conscious revolt.
H3988A.emploi: This verb appears 67 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the historical books, Proverbs, prophetic books, and Lamentations. It often describes the mutual rejection between the Lord and His people: Israel rejects His laws and commandments (Leviticus 26:15, Leviticus 26:43), while the Lord rejects Israel for its unfaithfulness (2 Kings 17:20, Psalms 78:59). The word is also used for social or personal rejection: despising the poor (Job 30:1), refusing divine correction (Proverbs 3:11), or abandoning a wife (Isaiah 54:6). The significance varies depending on the subject: when it is man who rejects, it is a fault; when it is God, it is a just consequence of disobedience.
H3988A.portee: This word confronts us with the seriousness of mutual rejection: that of man who deliberately refuses God and His word, and that of God who withdraws His support when His people persist in revolt. It is an invitation to take our covenant with God seriously and not to "despise" His words or His corrections. But it is also a call to humility: even when rejected, the Lord can call His people back, as He tells Israel in Isaiah 41:9.

sens: to flow losing its shape
to dissolve, to disintegrate
to disappear scattering
H3988B.detail:
1. The word primarily describes physical flow: something that flows or collapses like a liquid. In Job 7:5, the sick man's skin "dissolves," a strong image of the body disintegrating under illness.
2. From this comes the idea of disintegration: that which decomposes, loses its cohesion, falls apart. It is the image of a crusty earth that cracks and flows away.
3. Figuratively, it means to disappear or scatter: in Psalms 58:8, it is wished that the enemies "dissipate like waters that flow away," meaning that they go away, disperse, and are lost, without strength or substance.
H3988B.origine: The Hebrew word māas in the Niphal form (passive) evokes the fundamental image of flowing, like water that flows and runs off. This image also suggests dissolution, loss of shape and solidity. The word paints the idea that something solid becomes liquid and disappears.
H3988B.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible. In Job 7:5, it is in a cry of lament where the man afflicted by illness describes how his body disintegrates under sickness and worms. In Psalms 58:8, it is to call for judgment on the enemies: that they scatter and vanish like flowing water. In both cases, the image is of something losing its solidity and disappearing.
H3988B.portee: This word teaches the fragility of flesh and the power of enemies: just as water flows away, human strength dissolves, the body disintegrates, and the threat of the wicked can vanish. It is a call to trust in God rather than fear what ultimately collapses.

sens: food baked in the heat of the oven
baked grain offering presented to God
H3989.detail:
1. The word designates food prepared by being placed in the oven, thus baked by the dry heat of fire. In Leviticus 2:4, it refers to cakes or flatbreads made from flour kneaded with oil, baked in the oven and presented as an offering.
2. In the context of offerings to God, the term applies to a specific category of gifts: flour transformed by baking, making it a consumable and refined food, worthy of being offered to the Lord.
H3989.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to bake" or "to cook." It describes the action of transforming raw food by exposure to the heat of the oven. It is a concrete term that refers to a well-known domestic and culinary practice: baking in the oven, an important distinction in Israel where the common oven was a central element of village life.
H3989.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Leviticus 2:4. It is found in the passage that enumerates the different types of grain offerings that the Israelites could present to God. The baked offering was an alternative to other forms of offering (raw flour, pan-fried cakes). It represents a particular category of worship: gifts of flour transformed by heat, usually accompanied by oil.
H3989.portee: This term reminds us that offerings to God were not raw gifts, but foods prepared with care and transformation. Baking in the oven symbolizes human labor, effort, and refinement: it is a gift that cost time and work. It invites the believer to offer to God not what costs nothing, but what has been worked on and perfected.

sens: Deep darkness, absence of light
Figuratively: confusion, disorientation, uncertainty in the face of danger
In the history of salvation: the divine action that blinds God's enemies
H3990.detail:
1. Darkness refers to total obscurity, the absence of natural light. In the account of Joshua 24:7, God places darkness between the Israelites and the Egyptians pursuing them: this darkness separates the former, protecting them and blinding the latter, making pursuit impossible.

2. The word also evokes uncertainty and confusion: to be in darkness means not seeing where one is going, being disoriented in the face of impending danger. It is the experience of one who does not understand what is happening.

3. In the Bible, darkness often marks God's intervention to save His people: it is a sign of a mysterious divine action, a protection that escapes immediate human understanding.
H3990.origine: The Hebrew word מַאֲפֵל comes from a root that expresses the idea of darkness and blackness. It is related to the image of what is hidden, veiled, rendered invisible. In the Old Testament, darkness can be natural (night) or supernatural (the action of God), but it always retains this dimension of mystery and distance from light.
H3990.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 24:7, at the heart of the account of the crossing of the Red Sea. Joshua reminds the people how God acted: He placed darkness between Israel and Egypt, thus allowing the Hebrews to escape the pursuit of Pharaoh's chariots. It is a key moment in the history of salvation, where darkness becomes an instrument of divine deliverance rather than a symbol of misfortune.
H3990.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize that God sometimes acts in mystery and darkness, in a way invisible to human eyes. What seems confusing or dark may actually be divine protection. It is a lesson in trust: even when we do not clearly see God's action, it operates for our salvation.

sens: Deep and dense darkness
Total absence of light
Hostile and threatening environment
State of confusion or spiritual wandering
H3991.detail:
1. The word designates thick, compact darkness that cannot be pierced by sight: it is the image of complete night where all light is absent. In Jeremiah 2:31, the Lord asks Israel if He has been to them a desert or a land of thick darkness — the image emphasizes the absence of guidance and protection.
2. Figuratively, this darkness represents a world without reference points, without direction, where one cannot advance with confidence. It is the darkness of doubt and wandering.
3. For a believer, it also evokes the state of one who is separated from God, who does not see the way back and to grace — while God is precisely asking him: why do you refuse to return?
H3991.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of covering, enveloping, hence the image of darkness that envelops everything. It is constructed with the name formation prefix and combines with the idea of thickness and depth. The word describes a darkness that is not light or fleeting, but compact and oppressive.
H3991.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 2:31. It is found in a discourse where the Lord, through the prophet's mouth, exposes Israel's grievances: the people claim to be free and do not want to return to God, while the Lord questions them about their abandonment. The expression "thick darkness" contrasts with the light and direction that God could have offered, highlighting the people's responsibility in refusing this divine guidance.
H3991.portee: This word reminds the reader that distance from God is never neutral: it creates a state of confusion and loss. For today's believer, it invites not to be satisfied with a deceptive spiritual autonomy, but to recognize that without the presence and word of God, life remains in darkness. It is also a warning against voluntary blindness.

sens: Established for a long time, rooted, persistent
That which spreads or worsens gradually
Causing persistent pain or injury
That which irritates or hurts, figuratively
H3992.detail:
1. The word describes something ancient and inveterate, which has had time to settle deeply. In Leviticus 13:51 and 13:52, the leprous sore is said to be "inveterate" when it has spread on clothing or an object, showing that it does not disappear but persists and worsens: it is a rooted infection that renders the object permanently unclean.
2. The word can also describe what has established itself in a place and spreads there, as in Leviticus 14:44 where the "inveterate" sore in the house means a leprosy that has spread there and that nothing can stop.
3. Figuratively, the word expresses what hurts or causes pain durably. In Ezekiel 28:24, a thorn that "hurts" the house of Israel is a persistent irritation, a wound that one suffers from for a long time because of those who surround and despise Israel.
H3992.origine: The word comes from a root that fundamentally means "to hurt" or "to sting." The basic image is that of a thorn that pierces and wounds. Over time, the meaning has broadened to describe what persists, what has taken root and cannot be gotten rid of—like an old sore that does not heal or chronic pain. The Hebrew word emphasizes the idea of something that lasts and that one can no longer control.
H3992.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible. Three occurrences are found in Leviticus 13-14, in the laws concerning leprosy: it is the sore that has spread and can no longer be healed or purified, rendering the object or house permanently unclean. A fourth occurrence in Ezekiel 28:24 uses the word more figuratively: a thorn that hurts Israel, meaning a power (Egypt) that causes a persistent and humiliating wound. In all cases, the word evokes something durable, rooted, that cannot be gotten rid of and that continues to do harm.
H3992.portee: This word reminds us that sin and its consequences can become "inveterate": what starts small can take deep root and render our lives, families, or communities unclean and unusable if not addressed quickly. The image of the inveterate leprosy invites vigilance and repentance without delay, for an ignored wound spreads. It also invites recognition that some wounds and enmities, if they last, can continue to hurt for a long time.

sens: Hidden position from which one waits to surprise
Troop secretly posted to attack by surprise
Trap, unfair attack
H3993.detail:
1. An ambush is primarily a hidden place where one conceals oneself to observe without being seen and strike at the opportune moment. In Joshua 8:9, the Israelite warriors "place themselves in ambush between Bethel and Ai": they hide strategically waiting for the signal to rush upon the enemy.
2. It is also the group of soldiers who remain hidden to carry out the surprise attack. In Judges 9:35, "Abimelech and all the people who were with him rose from the ambush," suddenly springing forth to fight.
3. Figuratively, the ambush refers to any trap or scheme set up unfairly. In Psalms 10:8, the psalmist describes the wicked who "sits in ambush near the villages" to "murder the innocent"—an image of the predator stalking its defenseless prey.
H3993.origine: The Hebrew word מַאֲרָב (ma'arav) comes from the root אָרַב, which means "to hide" or "to set an ambush." This root evokes the idea of lurking, watching in silence. The word designates both the place and the act: it is the starting point of a military strategy where one sacrifices openness to win through cunning.
H3993.emploi: The word ambush (מַאֲרָב) appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always to describe a military strategy or a trap. In Joshua 8:9 and 2 Chronicles 13:13, it refers to war tactics: Joshua sets an ambush to defeat Ai, and Jeroboam uses the same stratagem against Judah. In Judges 9:35, it is Abimelech who emerges from the ambush. In Psalms 10:8, the context becomes moral: the ambush symbolizes the cunning of the wicked who spies on the innocent. The word thus retains its fundamental meaning—a surprise attack from a hidden position—but applies to both legitimate tactics and crime.
H3993.portee: The ambush reminds the reader that victory can be achieved through cunning as well as through strength: God approves Joshua's strategy. But in Psalms 10, it becomes the image of evil that hides and watches relentlessly. The term invites the believer to remain vigilant against the snares of sin and the enemy, while recognizing that divine wisdom can use indirect paths to accomplish its plans.

sens: Word or divine decision that brings misfortune and ruin upon someone
Material consequence of divine judgment: poverty, trouble, destruction
State of one who is rejected by God and subjected to His righteous anger
H3994.detail:
1. The curse is primarily a powerful word that comes from the mouth of God and strikes the one who receives it. It is a judgment pronounced against someone because of their sin or disobedience. In Deuteronomy 28:20, the Lord sends the curse, trouble, and threat against the people who transgress His covenant.
2. This word is not empty: it produces concrete and visible effects. The curse manifests itself through material misfortunes—sickness, poverty, failure in endeavors, progressive destruction. In Proverbs 3:33, the curse of the Lord dwells in the house of the wicked, while the blessing rests upon the dwelling of the righteous: two opposing destinies.
3. One who lives under the curse bears the weight of divine anger and suffers its consequences. In Proverbs 28:27 and Malachi 3:9, people are "struck by the curse"—they bear its yoke. It is the opposite of the blessing, which is the sign of God's favor.
H3994.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to execrate, to curse." The curse is an act of speech: to speak ill of someone, to pronounce a sentence against them. In Hebrew, to curse (אָרַר, arar) is to spit contempt, to reject someone from divine blessing. The curse is the exact opposite of the blessing (בְרָכָה, berakhah), which brings life and prosperity.
H3994.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the provided texts, all in the context of the covenant between God and Israel. The curse is the punishment that God promises for disobedience and sin. It appears especially in the speeches of blessing and curse (Deuteronomy 28), where it contrasts sharply with the blessing for the obedient. In Proverbs and Malachi, the curse is linked to ethical behavior: the wicked attract the curse, the righteous receive the blessing. It is never arbitrary, but always a just consequence of breaking the covenant or of injustice.
H3994.portee: The curse reminds us that God is not indifferent to sin: His justice is formidable, and it has real and visible consequences. But this doctrine also reveals God's goodness: He clearly warns of what awaits the disobedient, offering everyone the choice between blessing and curse. For the believer, understanding that God "curses" evil should strengthen their trust in divine judgment and their certainty that injustice will not go unpunished.

sens: Set apart, isolated from the rest
Distinctly separated in sharing or distribution
Belonging exclusively to someone, reserved for their exclusive use
H3995.detail:
1. The word designates what is isolated, removed from the whole. In Joshua 16:9, the cities of the sons of Ephraim are "separated" within the inheritance of the sons of Manasseh: they form distinct enclaves, non-contiguous, scattered in a territory that belongs to another people.
2. More broadly, it refers to what is clearly distinguished, set apart during a sharing or allocation. This suggests a deliberate intention to separate, to draw clear boundaries between what belongs to one and what belongs to another.
3. The underlying idea is that of what is reserved, destined exclusively: the separated cities belong solely to Ephraim, even if they are enclaved within the territory of Manasseh.
H3995.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the action of separating, dividing, distinguishing. This root evokes setting apart and demarcation. It is related to words that denote division, sharing, and distinction between things or people. The basic image is that of a boundary line, an intentional separation.
H3995.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Joshua 16:9. It specifically designates the cities that Ephraim possessed exclusively, even though they are geographically surrounded or scattered within the territory of Manasseh. It is a technical term used to describe the reality of the sharing of the promised land: the tribe of Ephraim receives cities that do not form a compact block but remain its legitimate possessions. The unique usage underscores the importance of this detail in the description of the territorial division after the conquest.
H3995.portee: This word reminds us that possessing an inheritance does not require contiguity or geographical proximity: God assigns to each what belongs to them, even if fragmented. For the believer, it is a lesson on divine sovereignty in the distribution of goods and the assurance that what is promised to us remains ours, regardless of external circumstances. The separation itself guarantees the identity and independence of each tribe in the sharing of the land.

sens: Passage through which one enters somewhere
Action of entering, penetrating a place
Door or access opening
Cardinal point west, direction of the sunset
Place of the sunset
H3996.detail:
1. The entry is primarily the physical passage, the door or opening through which one accesses a place: "He showed them how they could enter the city" (Judges 1:25). It is the path or access that allows crossing a boundary.
2. The word also designates the action of entering itself, the moment when someone crosses a threshold or enters a space: "when he enters your gates as one enters a conquered city" (Ezekiel 26:10). It is the movement of access.
3. Sometimes it designates the geographical point of access, as in "from the side of Gedor" (1 Chronicles 4:39), where the entry represents a direction or territorial boundary.
4. By a very ancient natural image, the word extends to the sunset: "the setting sun" (Joshua 1:4). The sun "enters" in a sense into the earth in the west.
5. Hence comes the meaning of the west itself, the direction where the sun disappears: "From the rising of the sun to its setting, let the name of the Lord be praised!" (Psalms 113:3), where "setting" means the west.
H3996.origine: The Hebrew word מָבוֹא (mavo) comes from the root בוא (bo), "to come, to enter." It is an action noun that literally means "a coming, an entry." The same root is found in many verbs of the New Testament translated into Greek (eiserchomaï) and expresses the idea of crossing, of passage from one side to the other. The extension of meaning towards "sunset" or "west" comes from a simple and universal image: the sun appears to "enter" the earth at the horizon, thus the "entry of the sun" naturally becomes the setting and the west.
H3996.emploi: The word מָבוֹא appears 22 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the historical and poetic books. Two uses dominate. First, the concrete, spatial entry: doors (2 Chronicles 23:15), passages to a city (Judges 1:25), or territorial boundaries (Joshua 1:4, Deuteronomy 11:30). It is the physical access that one crosses. Secondly, the sunset and the west: Psalms 113:3 ("From the rising of the sun to its setting"), Psalms 50:1 ("From the rising of the sun to its setting"), and the descriptions of Israel's borders where the "west" is marked by the sunset (Joshua 1:4, Joshua 23:4). The context always determines which meaning predominates.
H3996.portee: This word reminds us that in Scripture, all access, all progress begins with a door, a crossing. The entry can be a promise (the land that God gives) or a risk (entering a conquered city). For prayer and praise, it also evokes the universality of worship rendered to God: from the rising to the setting of the sun, it is to say that all creation, from one end to the other, must celebrate the Lord.

sens: Limit of a body of water, place where water touches land
Entry, passage through which one accesses a place
H3997.detail:
1. The edge is the limit where land meets water — here, it is the shore of the sea where Tyre is situated, like a city established at the junction between the sea and the continent. This image shows Tyre dominant, controlling maritime trade from this strategic position (Ezekiel 27:3).
2. This word can also designate an entry or access passage, the place through which one comes to a location. It is a natural image: just as the edge of the sea is the point where one arrives when coming from the sea, the edge is the threshold, the access.
H3997.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root "bo" (בא), which means "to enter, to come." The form "mévoah" is a noun derived from this root, literally designating "a coming towards" or "an arrival." In Hebrew, several words from the same family share this idea: "mavo" (מָבוֹא, "entry") is a very close variant. This root evokes natural movement: coming towards a place, accessing it.
H3997.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 27:3, where it designates the edge of the sea where Tyre rests. Tyre, a great Phoenician city, is described as sitting on this edge, dominant and magnificent. The context is a lamentation over this famous city, and the word emphasizes its remarkable geographical position: it is from this seashore that it extends its trade to peoples and islands. The word expresses both the physical location and the idea of access — Tyre is accessible, powerful, open to maritime trade.
H3997.portee: This word reminds us how geography shapes the destiny of cities and peoples. Tyre is beautiful and powerful because it is situated at the edge of the sea, a gateway to the world. For the reader, this invites reflection on how God places each one in a location that has meaning and significance. It is also an invitation to meditate on the pride of human powers: even the most beautifully placed city, in the most beautiful spot in the world, remains subject to God's judgment.

sens: State of mental trouble and disorder
Perplexity, disorientation in the face of an incomprehensible situation
Chaos and collective distress in the face of a catastrophe
H3998.detail:
1. Confusion is a state of deep disturbance where the mind is lost, where one no longer knows where one stands. It is the opposite of clarity and order. In Isaiah 22:5, confusion is part of the evils that will fall upon Jerusalem — along with trouble and crushing — when God sends His judgment: the walls collapse and cries of distress rise to the mountains.
2. Confusion also refers to disorientation, when one no longer understands what is happening, when events become incomprehensible and terrifying. In Micah 7:4, the prophet announces that those who refuse to listen to him will be struck by punishment and will find themselves in confusion — unable to grasp what is happening to them.
H3998.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of mixing, trouble, disorder. It is a concrete and vivid noun: confusion is not a mere philosophical abstraction, but the real experience of disarray that grips the mind and body. The word belongs to the vocabulary of divine judgment in the Bible: it is one of the consequences of rejecting God.
H3998.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both times in the prophets. In Isaiah 22:5, confusion is a judgment sent by the Lord upon Jerusalem on the day of the siege. In Micah 7:4, it strikes those who have turned away from justice. In both cases, it accompanies visible catastrophes — destruction, collapse — and it also describes the inner state of the victims: mental disorder, inability to understand or react. It is a rare word but loaded with meaning: it carries the weight of divine judgment.
H3998.portee: Confusion in the Bible is never a mere accident: it is the result of distancing from God and disobedience. It reminds us that without the wisdom of God, without obedience to His word, we are left to disorder and disarray. It is a powerful reason to remain attached to God and His commandments, which alone bring clarity and order to our lives.

sens: A catastrophic overflow of water that submerges the earth
The historical event of Noah's flood
Complete destruction by water
H3999.detail:
1. The flood is primarily a devastating rise of waters: they inundate the entire earth, engulf everything that lives, destroy all creation (Genesis 6:17). It is an unprecedented calamity in its scope.
2. The flood of Genesis is the specific event where God sent the waters to destroy the earth for forty days: they lifted the ark and submerged the entire inhabited earth (Genesis 7:17). This event marks a turning point in the history of humanity — before it and after it.
3. The flood also symbolizes God's judgment and the destruction that sin deserves: the waters will no longer return as a flood to destroy all flesh, God promises after the flood (Genesis 9:15). It is the very image of divine wrath that no longer tolerates iniquity.
H3999.origine: The Hebrew word mabbul literally denotes a flood, a submersion. It comes from the root that expresses the idea of overflowing, covering entirely. This word appears mainly in the accounts of Genesis to describe the cataclysm that God sent in the time of Noah. In biblical tradition, the flood becomes the founding event: it marks the destruction of sinful humanity and the new beginning after the ark.
H3999.emploi: The word appears about a dozen times in the Bible, concentrated in the account of Genesis (chapters 6 to 11) and once in the Psalms. It first describes the announcement of divine judgment: God declares that He will send the flood to destroy all flesh (Genesis 6:17). Then the text recounts its unfolding over forty days, with the waters rising and lifting the ark (Genesis 7:17). After the flood, the notion becomes a chronological marker: what happened 'after the flood' is mentioned (Genesis 10:1, 11:10). It also marks the transition between the old humanity and the new covenant: God promises that the waters will no longer be a flood to destroy (Genesis 9:15). In the Psalms, the flood becomes the image of God's power and judgment (Psalms 29:10).
H3999.portee: The flood teaches the believer the reality of God's judgment against sin and His determination to purify creation. It is also a hidden act of mercy: God saves Noah and his family, showing that even in judgment, grace remains. For the modern reader, the flood reminds us that God takes evil and rebellion seriously, but He always offers a way of escape to those who believe and obey.
